items.title: What is a Stock Exchange? Meaning, Role and Indian Examples
items.description: Stock exchange meaning explained simply: how NSE and BSE match buy and sell orders, who can trade on them and how SEBI regulates exchanges in India.
items.short: A stock exchange is a regulated marketplace where buy and sell orders for listed securities are matched electronically under rules approved by the market regulator.
body: In India the two national stock exchanges for equities are the National Stock Exchange (NSE) and BSE (formerly the Bombay Stock Exchange). Commodity derivatives trade mainly on MCX and NCDEX, while NSE and BSE also run segments for equity derivatives, currency derivatives and debt. Every exchange is recognised by SEBI under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956.

An exchange does not buy or sell shares itself. It provides an anonymous order-matching system: orders from thousands of brokers flow into an order book, and the system matches them on price-time priority — the best price first, and at the same price, the earliest order first. The exchange also sets trading hours, price bands, surveillance rules and listing requirements for companies.

Ordinary investors cannot place orders directly on the exchange. They must go through a SEBI-registered stock broker who is a trading member of that exchange. After a trade is matched, the exchange's clearing corporation takes over to settle it, so the buyer gets shares and the seller gets money even if the counterparty fails.

A common confusion is to treat 'the market' and 'the exchange' as the same thing. The exchange is the infrastructure; prices are set by the buyers and sellers using it. Another is assuming a share listed on BSE cannot be sold on NSE — many large companies are listed on both, and a share bought on one exchange can usually be sold on the other because the holding sits in your demat account, not with the exchange.
items.example: Suppose at 10:15 a.m. the NSE order book for a stock shows the best buy order at ₹501.50 for 200 shares and the best sell order at ₹502.00 for 150 shares. No trade happens until someone crosses the gap. If you place a market buy order for 100 shares, the system matches you instantly against the ₹502.00 sell order, leaving 50 shares at that price for the next buyer. Your broker receives the trade confirmation within seconds.
faqs: How many stock exchanges are there in India?

There are a few SEBI-recognised exchanges, but almost all equity trading happens on NSE and BSE. MCX and NCDEX dominate commodity derivatives, and the Metropolitan Stock Exchange (MSE) is a smaller national exchange. Most older regional exchanges have exited. For the current list, check SEBI's website under recognised stock exchanges.
Can I buy shares without a stock exchange?

Off-market transfers between two people are possible through depository instructions, for example gifting shares to a family member. But for buying from the general public at market prices, you need a broker and an exchange. Unlisted shares can be traded privately, but without the price discovery, liquidity and settlement guarantee an exchange provides.

items.title: Primary Market vs Secondary Market: Meaning and Differences
items.description: Understand the difference between primary and secondary markets in India — IPOs, FPOs and rights issues versus trading on NSE and BSE — with a simple example.
items.short: The primary market is where companies issue new securities to raise money; the secondary market is where investors trade existing securities among themselves on stock exchanges.
body: When a company sells shares or bonds for the first time — through an IPO, a follow-on offer, a rights issue, a private placement or a QIP — the money goes to the company (or to selling shareholders in an offer for sale). That is the primary market, sometimes called the new issue market. Merchant bankers, registrars, underwriters and bankers to the issue are the key intermediaries here.

Once those securities are listed, they trade on exchanges such as NSE and BSE. That is the secondary market. Here the company receives nothing: if you buy 100 shares of a listed bank, your money goes to another investor who was selling. Stock brokers, clearing corporations and depositories are the main intermediaries.

The two markets depend on each other. Investors are willing to subscribe in the primary market because they know they can later exit in the secondary market. And secondary market prices tell companies how much investors value them, which affects the price at which they can raise fresh capital.

A frequent exam trap: an offer for sale (OFS) through the exchange window happens on the exchange platform, yet the shares are existing ones sold by promoters, and the company does not get the money. Similarly, a bonus issue creates new shares but raises no money, so it is not a fund-raising primary issue at all.
items.example: A company raises ₹500 crore through an IPO by issuing 2 crore new shares at ₹250 each — that ₹500 crore reaches the company's bank account (minus issue expenses). A month after listing, the share trades at ₹310 on NSE. An investor who sells 1,000 shares at ₹310 receives ₹3,10,000 from another investor; the company's cash balance does not change by a single rupee.
faqs: Is an IPO part of the primary or secondary market?

An IPO is a primary market transaction because the shares are being issued for the first time. However, many Indian IPOs combine a fresh issue (money goes to the company) with an offer for sale (money goes to existing shareholders). Both parts happen in the primary market, but only the fresh issue portion raises capital for the business.
Why is the secondary market important if the company gets no money?

It gives investors liquidity and continuous price discovery. Without a place to sell, few people would invest in new issues. A healthy secondary market also lets companies judge investor appetite and raise money later through follow-on offers, QIPs or rights issues at prices linked to the market value.

items.title: What is a Depository? NSDL and CDSL Meaning Explained
items.description: Depository meaning in the Indian stock market: how NSDL and CDSL hold shares in electronic form, their role in settlement and how they differ from DPs.
items.short: A depository is a SEBI-registered institution that holds securities in electronic (dematerialised) form for investors and records every transfer of ownership by book entry.
body: India has two depositories: National Securities Depository Ltd (NSDL), set up in 1996, and Central Depository Services (India) Ltd (CDSL), set up in 1999. They are governed by the Depositories Act, 1996 and SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Regulations. Before them, shares existed as paper certificates that had to be physically transferred, signed and sent to the company — a process prone to forgery, loss and delays.

A depository works much like a bank for securities. Just as a bank holds your money and moves it between accounts by entries in its books, a depository holds your shares, bonds, mutual fund units and government securities and transfers them by debiting one demat account and crediting another. No paper changes hands.

Investors do not deal with the depository directly. They open a demat account with a depository participant (DP) — a bank, broker or financial institution registered as an agent of NSDL or CDSL. The DP provides the account, statements and service; the depository maintains the master record. In company records, the depository is shown as the registered owner, while you are the beneficial owner with all economic and voting rights.

Depositories also support pledges, corporate actions such as bonus and dividend credits, freezing of accounts, nomination and electronic voting. Their role in settlement is critical: on settlement day the clearing corporation instructs the depositories to move shares from sellers to buyers.
items.example: Ravi holds 50 shares of a company in his CDSL demat account through his broker-DP. He sells them on NSE on Monday. Under T+1 settlement, the shares are debited from his account and delivered to the clearing corporation, which passes them to the buyer's DP on Tuesday. The buyer may hold an NSDL account — the two depositories are interconnected, so the inter-depository transfer happens automatically without either investor doing anything extra.
faqs: What is the difference between NSDL and CDSL?

Functionally they do the same job and are interoperable. The differences are in ownership and history: NSDL was promoted mainly by IDBI, UTI and NSE, while CDSL was promoted by BSE along with banks. Your choice usually depends on which depository your broker or bank DP is linked with, not on any difference in safety.
Does the depository hold my money too?

No. A depository holds only securities. Money from sales goes through your broker and the clearing corporation to your bank account. Keeping this distinction clear helps in exams: depositories deal with securities transfer, clearing corporations handle funds and securities settlement obligations, and banks handle cash.

items.title: Depository Participant (DP) Meaning, Role and Charges
items.description: What a depository participant does: opening demat accounts, processing delivery instructions and pledges, and how DPs link investors to NSDL or CDSL.
items.short: A depository participant (DP) is a SEBI-registered agent of NSDL or CDSL through which investors open and operate demat accounts.
body: The depository keeps the master records, but it does not deal with millions of individual investors. That front-office role belongs to depository participants. Banks, stock brokers, custodians and some financial institutions register with SEBI as DPs and connect to either NSDL, CDSL or both. Each DP is identified by a DP ID, and your demat account number combines the DP ID with your client ID.

A DP's services include opening accounts after KYC, processing delivery instruction slips (DIS) or electronic instructions to transfer shares, handling pledge and unpledge requests, dematerialising physical certificates, issuing transaction and holding statements, updating nominations and bank details, and closing or transferring accounts.

DPs charge fees such as account maintenance charges and per-transaction debit charges. These are set by each DP within the framework of the depository, so they vary. Many brokers offer a Basic Services Demat Account (BSDA) for small holders with reduced or nil maintenance charges, subject to holding-value limits that SEBI revises from time to time — check the current limit on SEBI's or your DP's website.

A common misconception is that if your DP or broker shuts down, your shares are lost. Your holdings are recorded at the depository in your name; if a DP exits, accounts are shifted to another DP. Equally, a DP cannot move shares out of your account without a valid instruction — either a signed slip, an online authorisation or a DDPI you have given for specific purposes.
items.example: Meena's demat account number is IN30xxxx12345678 on NSDL: the first eight characters (IN30xxxx) are the DP ID of her bank, and the last eight digits are her client ID. She buys shares through a discount broker but wants delivery in her existing bank demat account. She gives the broker her full NSDL account number; after T+1 settlement, the bank DP credits the shares and her monthly holding statement shows them.
faqs: Can I have demat accounts with more than one DP?

Yes. An investor can hold several demat accounts with different DPs, even across NSDL and CDSL, using the same PAN. Each account carries its own charges and statements. Many people consolidate to reduce maintenance fees and simplify tracking, which can be done by transferring holdings to one account and closing the others.
What is a delivery instruction slip (DIS)?

A DIS is the instruction an account holder gives the DP to debit securities from their demat account, for example for an off-market transfer or delivery against a sale. It used to be a pre-numbered paper booklet; today most instructions are given electronically with OTP or TPIN-based authentication, or through a DDPI for broker-linked sales.

items.title: What is a Demat Account? Meaning, Types and How It Works
items.description: Demat account meaning in simple words: how shares are held electronically, types of demat accounts in India, and how a demat differs from a trading account.
items.short: A demat account is an account with a depository participant that holds shares, bonds, ETFs and other securities in electronic form instead of paper certificates.
body: 'Demat' is short for dematerialised. Since SEBI made delivery in demat form compulsory for listed shares, and transfers of physical shares were stopped in 2019 (except transmission and transposition), anyone who buys listed securities in India needs a demat account. You open it with a DP after completing KYC, and it is linked to your PAN and bank account.

A demat account is not where you place orders — that is the trading account with your broker. Think of it this way: the trading account is the shop counter, the demat account is your locker. When you buy, shares land in the demat; when you sell, they leave it. Many brokers open both together, which is why people mix them up.

Main types include the regular demat account for resident Indians, the Basic Services Demat Account (BSDA) for small investors with lower charges, and repatriable and non-repatriable demat accounts for NRIs. A demat can be held singly or jointly (up to three holders), and nomination can be registered or explicitly opted out of.

Besides equity shares, a demat account can hold ETFs, government securities, sovereign gold bonds, corporate bonds, debentures and mutual fund units. Corporate benefits such as bonus shares, split shares and rights entitlements are credited directly, while dividends go to the linked bank account.
items.example: Anil buys 40 shares of a company at ₹1,250 on Wednesday through his trading account, paying ₹50,000 plus charges. On Thursday (T+1) the 40 shares appear in his demat account. Two months later the company announces a 1:1 bonus; on the credit date his demat shows 80 shares with no action needed from him. When he later sells 30 shares, the demat balance falls to 50 after the sale settles.
faqs: Is a demat account the same as a trading account?

No. A trading account with a broker is used to place buy and sell orders on the exchange. A demat account with a DP stores the securities. You need both to trade in the stock market, but you need only a demat account to receive IPO allotments, gifts or transfers, or to hold securities you already own.
Can I hold physical share certificates now?

You can still own them, but transfers of physical shares of listed companies are no longer allowed except in limited cases such as transmission on death. To sell, you must first dematerialise the certificates through your DP, which sends them to the company's registrar for verification and then credits your demat account.

items.title: What is ISIN? Meaning, Format and Example in India
items.description: ISIN meaning explained: the 12-character code that identifies every security in a demat account, how Indian ISINs are structured and why they matter.
items.short: An ISIN is a unique 12-character alphanumeric code that identifies a specific security, such as a share, bond or mutual fund unit, across markets and depositories.
body: ISIN follows the international standard ISO 6166. In India, NSDL allots ISINs for equity, debt, government securities and mutual fund units (with CDSL also using them), so every holding in your demat account carries one. Exchanges, depositories, registrars and custodians use the ISIN rather than the company name, because names change and similar names can cause errors.

The structure is fixed: two letters for the country (IN for India), nine characters that identify the issuer and the type of security, and a final check digit calculated from the other characters to catch typing mistakes. For Indian equities, the third character is usually 'E' and many equity ISINs end with a segment showing the share type, while debt, government securities and mutual fund units follow their own patterns.

The important point is that an ISIN identifies a particular security, not a company. One company can have many ISINs: its equity shares, partly paid shares, each bond series and each type of debenture get separate codes. Similarly, each plan and option of a mutual fund scheme has its own ISIN.

ISINs can change after certain corporate actions, for example when partly paid shares become fully paid, or after a face-value change in some cases. Investors usually notice this when a holding temporarily appears twice or under a new code in their statement.
items.example: A company has equity shares with ISIN beginning INE and also two non-convertible debenture series. In the investor's demat statement, the equity holding of 100 shares and the 50 debentures show under three different ISINs, even though all carry the same company name. When the investor gives an off-market transfer instruction for 20 equity shares, the DP asks for the equity ISIN — quoting a debenture ISIN would move the wrong security.
faqs: Is ISIN the same as the stock symbol?

No. A symbol like a short ticker is an exchange-specific trading code that can differ between NSE and BSE (BSE also uses numeric scrip codes). The ISIN is the same everywhere and is used for settlement and depository records. In exams, remember: symbol for trading screens, ISIN for depository identification.
Where can I find the ISIN of a security?

Your demat holding statement and contract notes show it. You can also search the NSDL ISIN database, exchange websites, the company's investor relations page or a mutual fund's factsheet. Always match the ISIN when transferring securities or filling corporate action forms.

items.title: What is an IPO? Initial Public Offering Meaning with Example
items.description: IPO meaning in the share market: how an initial public offering works in India, investor categories, the timeline from bidding to listing and common myths.
items.short: An initial public offering (IPO) is the first sale of a company's shares to the public, after which the shares are listed and traded on stock exchanges.
body: A company goes public to raise capital for expansion or debt repayment, to let early investors and promoters sell part of their stake, and to gain the visibility and liquidity of a listed share. An IPO can have a fresh issue (new shares, money to the company), an offer for sale (existing shares, money to sellers), or both.

The process is governed by the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018. The company appoints merchant bankers (book running lead managers), files a draft red herring prospectus with SEBI, receives observations, and then opens the issue — typically for three working days. Most IPOs use book building, where investors bid within a price band.

Bids are divided into categories: qualified institutional buyers (QIBs), non-institutional investors (NIIs) and retail individual investors, plus sometimes employee and shareholder quotas. Retail investors bid up to ₹2 lakh. Payment is through ASBA, so money is only blocked, not debited, until allotment. Listing now happens on T+3 — three working days after the issue closes (as of 2026; check SEBI circulars).

Two misconceptions are common. First, oversubscription does not mean you will get shares; in retail, allotment is by lottery to give as many applicants as possible one minimum lot. Second, the IPO price is not a 'fair' value certified by SEBI — SEBI reviews disclosures, not the price, and listing-day prices can be above or below the issue price.
items.example: A company offers shares in a price band of ₹270–₹285 with a lot size of 52 shares. A retail investor bids for 3 lots at the cut-off price, so the ASBA block is 3 × 52 × ₹285 = ₹44,460. The retail portion is subscribed 20 times. The investor is allotted one lot in the lottery at the final price of ₹285, so ₹14,820 is debited and the remaining ₹29,640 block is released.
faqs: What is the minimum amount to apply in an IPO?

The minimum is one lot, and SEBI requires the minimum application value to fall within a prescribed range, so it is usually around ₹14,000–₹15,000 for mainboard IPOs. The exact amount depends on the lot size and price band printed in the RHP and issue advertisement. SME IPOs have much larger minimum lots.
What is the cut-off price in an IPO?

Retail and employee applicants can tick 'cut-off', meaning they agree to buy at whatever final price is fixed within the band. Their block is calculated at the upper end of the band. If the final price is lower, the extra amount is unblocked. Institutions and NIIs cannot bid at cut-off; they must specify a price.

items.title: Book Building Process in IPO: Meaning, Price Band, Cut-off
items.description: Book building meaning in IPOs: how a price band, investor bids and demand at each price help fix the final issue price, compared with a fixed price issue.
items.short: Book building is a price-discovery method in public issues where investors bid within a price band and the final issue price is set based on the demand recorded at each price.
body: In a fixed price issue, the company announces one price in advance and investors simply apply. In book building, the company announces a price band — the upper end can be at most 120% of the lower end (floor), and in practice bands are much narrower. Investors bid the quantity and price they are willing to pay, and all bids are recorded in an electronic 'book' maintained by the book running lead managers.

When bidding closes, the lead managers and the company study the demand curve: how many shares are demanded at each price. The final issue price is usually set at the highest price at which the entire issue can be sold, often the top of the band when demand is strong. Bids below the final price are rejected; bids at or above it are eligible for allotment at the final price.

SEBI rules reserve portions for different categories. In a typical book-built IPO by a company meeting the profitability track-record test, not more than 50% goes to QIBs, at least 35% to retail investors and at least 15% to non-institutional investors. Companies that do not meet the profitability test must allot at least 75% to QIBs, and the retail share falls to at most 10%.

Book building is preferred because it reflects actual demand rather than a guess by the issuer. Its weakness is that institutional demand can strongly influence the price, and a high subscription number may simply reflect leveraged or speculative applications.
items.example: An issue of 1,00,00,000 shares has a band of ₹100–₹108. Bids received: 40 lakh shares at ₹108, 50 lakh more at ₹106 and above, and 30 lakh more at ₹100–₹105. Cumulative demand at ₹106 or higher is 90 lakh — short of 1 crore. At ₹105 and above, demand might reach 1.05 crore, so the issue can be fully sold at ₹105. Bids below ₹105 are rejected and everyone allotted pays ₹105.
faqs: What is the difference between a fixed price issue and book building?

In a fixed price issue the price is known when you apply, and demand is disclosed only after closing. In book building the price band is known, the final price is decided after bidding, and demand is visible during the bidding period. Most large Indian IPOs today use book building.
Who maintains the book in book building?

The book running lead managers (merchant bankers) appointed by the issuer manage the process. Bids are entered by syndicate members, brokers, DPs, registrars and banks into the exchanges' electronic bidding platforms, which provide a consolidated demand picture. The final price is decided by the issuer in consultation with the lead managers.

items.title: Red Herring Prospectus (RHP) Meaning and DRHP Difference
items.description: What a red herring prospectus is, why it lacks the final price, how it differs from the DRHP and final prospectus, and which sections to read.
items.short: A red herring prospectus is the offer document for a book-built issue that contains full disclosures about the company but not the final issue price or exact number of shares.
body: The name comes from the practice of printing a warning on the cover in red, signalling that some details are incomplete. In a book-built IPO the price is discovered only after bidding, so the document filed before the issue opens cannot state it. It does state the price band (announced separately before opening), the issue size in rupees or shares, and all other disclosures required under SEBI's ICDR Regulations.

The sequence is: Draft Red Herring Prospectus (DRHP) filed with SEBI for observations and made public for comments → Red Herring Prospectus (RHP) filed with the Registrar of Companies before the issue opens → final Prospectus filed after the price is fixed, adding the issue price and the number of shares.

For investors, the RHP is the single most useful document. Key sections are risk factors, objects of the issue (how the money will be used), the offer structure, financial statements, outstanding litigation, promoter and group company details, and the basis for issue price, which compares valuation ratios with listed peers.

A common mistake is to read only media summaries or the abridged prospectus attached to forms. The abridged version is useful but short; contingent liabilities, related-party transactions and restated financial notes are often only in the full RHP, available on SEBI, exchange and lead-manager websites.
items.example: A company files its DRHP in January proposing a ₹1,200 crore IPO: ₹800 crore fresh issue and ₹400 crore OFS. After SEBI observations, it files the RHP in May, and two days before opening announces a band of ₹440–₹463. The issue is subscribed and priced at ₹463, so the final prospectus records the fresh issue as about 1.73 crore shares (₹800 crore ÷ ₹463 ≈ 1,72,78,618 shares).
faqs: Is a DRHP approved by SEBI?

SEBI does not 'approve' an offer document or vouch for the company. It issues observations on whether disclosures are adequate, and the issuer must address them before filing the RHP. Every offer document carries a disclaimer saying SEBI does not take responsibility for the financial soundness of the project or correctness of statements.
Why is it called a red herring prospectus?

The term comes from US practice, where the preliminary prospectus carried a cautionary statement printed in red ink on the cover. It warned that the document was not final and that pricing and some details would be added later. The name stuck, and Indian law uses it for book-built issues.

items.title: ASBA Meaning: How Blocked Amount Works in IPO Applications
items.description: ASBA explained: how your IPO money stays in your bank account but is blocked until allotment, UPI mandates, SCSBs and what happens if no shares are allotted.
items.short: ASBA is the mandatory process for public issue applications in which the application money stays in the investor's bank account but is blocked until shares are allotted.
body: Before ASBA, investors paid by cheque and waited weeks for refunds if they got nothing. Under ASBA, a self-certified syndicate bank (SCSB) blocks the bid amount in the investor's account. The money keeps earning savings interest and cannot be used for anything else while blocked. On allotment, only the amount for allotted shares is debited, and the balance is unblocked.

Individual investors can apply in two main ways. They can use net banking ASBA directly with their bank, or apply through a broker, DP, registrar or app using the UPI mechanism, where the investor approves a UPI mandate on their phone to block funds. UPI-based applications have a value limit for individuals — ₹5 lakh as of 2026; check current SEBI rules.

ASBA is compulsory for all public issues: IPOs, FPOs, rights issues and public issues of debt. One PAN can submit only one application per category in an IPO; multiple applications with the same PAN are rejected, which is why using different apps does not increase your chances.

Common confusion: a mandate request that is not approved before the cut-off time means no application at all. Also, the blocked amount is visible in your bank as a 'lien' or reduced available balance — it is not a payment, and you do not need to request a refund if nothing is allotted.
items.example: Priya applies for 2 lots of 60 shares in an IPO with a band of ₹235–₹248, bidding at cut-off. Her bank blocks 2 × 60 × ₹248 = ₹29,760 via UPI mandate. Final price is ₹248 and she gets 1 lot. On allotment day ₹14,880 is debited and ₹14,880 is unblocked. Had she received nothing, the full ₹29,760 would simply have been unblocked.
faqs: What is an SCSB?

A self-certified syndicate bank is a SEBI-registered banker to an issue that offers ASBA facility — accepting applications, blocking funds and transferring money on allotment. Most large commercial banks are SCSBs. The list, along with branches that accept physical ASBA forms and banks that support UPI, is published on SEBI's website.
Does ASBA apply to rights issues?

Yes. Shareholders applying in rights issues also use ASBA, and SEBI has moved rights issues to a largely electronic process where rights entitlements are credited to demat accounts and can be traded. Applying through ASBA means the money stays in your account until shares are allotted.

items.title: Anchor Investor in IPO: Meaning, Lock-in and Allocation
items.description: Who anchor investors are, how much of an IPO they can take, their lock-in period and why anchor demand is watched closely before an issue opens.
items.short: An anchor investor is a qualified institutional buyer who commits a large amount to a book-built IPO one working day before the issue opens to the public.
body: Anchor investors were introduced by SEBI to give an IPO a stable base of committed institutional money and to signal demand to other investors. Under the ICDR Regulations, an anchor investor must be a QIB and must apply for at least ₹10 crore. Up to 60% of the QIB portion can be allotted to anchors, and one-third of the anchor portion is reserved for domestic mutual funds.

The anchor book is opened a day before the public issue. The anchor price is fixed within the price band, and allotment is announced through an exchange filing listing each anchor and the number of shares. If the final issue price later turns out higher than the anchor price, anchors must pay the difference; if it is lower, they do not get a refund.

To discourage quick flipping, anchor shares carry a lock-in: 50% of the shares cannot be sold for 30 days from allotment and the remaining 50% for 90 days (as of 2026; confirm in current ICDR rules). These lock-in expiry dates are often followed by heavy selling and price moves, which traders watch.

A misconception is that strong anchor participation guarantees listing gains. Anchors take a view based on their own horizon and allocation needs; anchors in many issues have seen listing prices below the issue price. Retail investors should still read the RHP rather than rely only on anchor names.
items.example: An IPO's QIB portion is ₹600 crore. Up to 60%, or ₹360 crore, can go to anchors, of which one-third (₹120 crore) is reserved for domestic mutual funds. Say 18 anchors are allotted at ₹410 per share. Each must invest at least ₹10 crore. One fund receiving 3,65,853 shares (≈₹15 crore) can sell 1,82,926 shares after 30 days and the rest only after 90 days.
faqs: Is the anchor portion part of the QIB quota?

Yes. The anchor allocation comes out of the QIB portion, not in addition to it. Any shares not taken by anchors are added back to the QIB category for the public bidding period. So when you see the QIB subscription number, remember it often refers to the non-anchor part of the QIB book.
Can an anchor investor withdraw its bid?

No. Anchor investors cannot withdraw or lower their bids after the anchor bidding day, which is what makes their commitment meaningful. Like other QIBs and non-institutional investors in an IPO, they are also not allowed to revise bids downward during the issue.

items.title: QIB Meaning: Qualified Institutional Buyer Examples in India
items.description: What a qualified institutional buyer is under SEBI rules, which entities qualify, the QIB quota in IPOs and how QIB subscription is read by investors.
items.short: A qualified institutional buyer (QIB) is a large, sophisticated institutional investor recognised by SEBI's ICDR Regulations as eligible for the QIB category in issues.
body: The QIB definition lists categories of institutions presumed to have the expertise and resources to evaluate issues. They include mutual funds, foreign portfolio investors (excluding individuals, corporate bodies and family offices), scheduled commercial banks, insurance companies, public financial institutions, multilateral and bilateral development institutions, alternative investment funds and venture capital funds, and pension and provident funds above a minimum corpus size.

QIBs get a reserved portion in book-built IPOs — up to 50% for companies with a profitability track record, and at least 75% for those without. Within the QIB portion, 5% (excluding the anchor part) is set aside for mutual funds. QIBs must bid with a price, cannot bid at cut-off, and cannot withdraw or lower their bids once placed.

QIB status also matters for other routes. A qualified institutions placement (QIP) can be made only to QIBs, and certain debt issues and institutional trading platforms are restricted to them. Allotment to QIBs in an IPO is proportionate, unlike the lottery used for retail investors.

The QIB subscription figure is closely tracked because institutions do detailed research. But it is not a quality certificate; high QIB demand can reflect index inclusion needs or allocation strategy rather than a judgement on value. And an individual, however wealthy, cannot be a QIB — high-net-worth individuals fall in the non-institutional category.
items.example: An IPO of ₹1,000 crore by a profitable company reserves ₹500 crore for QIBs, ₹150 crore for NIIs and ₹350 crore for retail. If ₹300 crore of the QIB portion goes to anchors, ₹200 crore remains, of which 5% (₹10 crore) is reserved for mutual funds. If QIBs bid for ₹9,000 crore against ₹200 crore, the QIB portion is subscribed 45 times and each QIB gets roughly 1/45th of its bid.
faqs: Is an HNI a QIB?

No. High-net-worth individuals and most companies bidding above ₹2 lakh fall in the non-institutional investor (NII) category. QIB status depends on the type of institution as listed in SEBI's ICDR Regulations, not on wealth. Some family offices and corporate bodies registered as FPIs are also specifically excluded.
Why can't QIBs withdraw bids in an IPO?

SEBI barred QIB and NII withdrawals to stop large investors from creating an artificial impression of demand early in the issue and then pulling out. Because others may rely on the subscription data, institutional bids must stay firm. Retail investors, by contrast, can modify or cancel bids during the bidding period.

items.title: Green Shoe Option in IPO: Meaning and Price Stabilisation
items.description: Green shoe option explained: over-allotment of up to 15%, the stabilising agent's role after listing, and what happens if the share price rises or falls.
items.short: A green shoe option lets an issuer allot shares beyond the issue size and use the extra money to support the share price after listing through a stabilising agent.
body: The name comes from the Green Shoe Manufacturing Company, the first US issuer to use the mechanism. Under SEBI's ICDR Regulations, an issuer can over-allot up to 15% of the issue size. The extra shares are borrowed from the promoters, and one of the merchant bankers is appointed as the stabilising agent (SA).

The money received from the over-allotted shares goes into a separate account. During the stabilisation period — up to 30 days from listing — if the market price falls below the issue price, the SA uses this money to buy shares from the market. This buying creates support and limits the fall. The shares bought are returned to the promoters to close the borrowing.

If the price stays above the issue price, the SA has no reason to buy. Instead, the company issues fresh shares to the promoters equal to the over-allotted quantity, effectively completing a larger issue. Any combination is possible: the SA may buy back some shares and the company issues the rest.

The mechanism is rare in Indian IPOs but frequently appears in exam questions. It is often confused with an oversubscription retention, where an issuer keeps excess money from a debt issue. A green shoe is about post-listing price stabilisation, not simply keeping excess subscription.
items.example: A company issues 1 crore shares at ₹200 with a green shoe of 15 lakh shares borrowed from the promoter, so investors receive 1.15 crore shares and ₹30 crore sits with the stabilising agent. After listing the price drops to ₹188. The SA buys 10 lakh shares at an average ₹190 (₹19 crore) and returns them to the promoter. The company then issues the remaining 5 lakh shares to the promoter and receives ₹10 crore from the account; the ₹1 crore surplus goes to the exchange's investor protection and education fund.
faqs: Who decides whether to use the green shoe option?

The issuer decides to include a green shoe in the offer document, and the stabilising agent — normally one of the lead managers — decides when and how much to buy after listing, within the rules. All stabilisation activity must be reported to the exchanges and disclosed after the period ends.
What happens to the profits from stabilisation?

Any surplus in the stabilisation account after closing, net of expenses, is not kept by the issuer or the stabilising agent. Under SEBI rules it must be transferred to the investor protection and education fund of the exchanges. This removes any incentive to profit from stabilising.

items.title: Offer for Sale (OFS) Meaning and Stock Exchange Window
items.description: Offer for sale meaning in the share market: how promoters sell shares via the OFS window, floor price, retail quota and how it differs from a fresh issue.
items.short: An offer for sale is a sale of existing shares by promoters or other shareholders to the public, where the selling shareholders, not the company, receive the money.
body: The term appears in two settings. In an IPO, the OFS component lets existing shareholders such as private equity funds and promoters sell part of their holding alongside or instead of a fresh issue. The proceeds go to the sellers, so the company's capital does not change. Investors read the RHP to see how much of an IPO is OFS versus fresh issue.

The second setting is the OFS through stock exchange mechanism for already listed companies. SEBI introduced it so promoters of listed companies can sell shares quickly — for example to meet the 25% minimum public shareholding requirement, or for government disinvestment. A separate exchange window is used, and the seller announces a floor price at least one trading day in advance.

In the exchange route, at least 10% of the offer is reserved for retail investors (bids up to ₹2 lakh), who may bid at the cut-off price, and at least 25% is reserved for mutual funds and insurance companies. Non-retail bids typically happen on day T and retail bids on day T+1. Allotment is by price priority for non-retail investors, and settlement follows normal exchange settlement.

Common confusion: an OFS uses the exchange platform, which makes it look like secondary market trading, but the floor price is often at a discount to the market price to attract bidders. Also, the government's disinvestment sales of PSU shares often use this window, which is why OFS is frequent in news.
items.example: The government plans to sell 3% of a PSU with 100 crore shares, i.e. 3 crore shares, at a floor price of ₹420 when the market price is ₹445 — a discount of about 5.6%. Retail investors get at least 10%, or 30 lakh shares. A retail investor bidding for 470 shares at cut-off uses ₹1,97,400 (₹420 × 470), within the ₹2 lakh retail limit.
faqs: Does the company get money in an offer for sale?

No. In an OFS, existing shares change hands, so the proceeds go to the selling shareholders. The company only receives money through a fresh issue of shares. In an IPO that combines both, check the 'objects of the issue' section of the RHP, which explains the use of the fresh issue proceeds only.
Who can sell through the OFS window?

Promoters and promoter group entities of eligible listed companies, and in some cases non-promoter shareholders holding a significant stake, can use the OFS mechanism, subject to SEBI's eligibility conditions such as minimum offer size and market capitalisation thresholds. These conditions are revised from time to time, so check the latest SEBI circular.

items.title: What is a Rights Issue? Meaning, Ratio and Ex-Rights Price
items.description: Rights issue meaning with example: how existing shareholders get new shares at a discount, rights entitlements in demat, renunciation and ex-rights price.
items.short: A rights issue is an offer of new shares by a listed company to its existing shareholders, in proportion to their current holding, usually at a discount to the market price.
body: Rights issues let a company raise capital while giving existing shareholders the first chance to maintain their percentage ownership. The offer is made in a ratio such as 1:5, meaning one new share for every five held on the record date. Under the Companies Act, 2013, the offer must remain open for a minimum period, and shareholders may accept, decline or renounce their rights in favour of others.

SEBI has made the process largely electronic. Rights entitlements (REs) are credited to shareholders' demat accounts under a separate ISIN and can be traded on the exchange during the renunciation period. A shareholder who does not want to invest can sell the REs instead of letting them lapse. Applications are made through ASBA.

Because the new shares come at a discount, the market price usually adjusts after the record date. The theoretical ex-rights price (TERP) is the weighted average of the old price and the rights price across old and new shares. A shareholder who neither subscribes nor sells the REs suffers dilution and an effective loss in value.

Many investors think a rights issue at a discount is 'free money'. It is not: you must pay to subscribe, and the discount is offset by the fall in price after the issue. Rights issues also differ from bonus issues, which involve no payment, and from preferential allotments, which go only to selected investors.
items.example: A company's share trades at ₹300. It announces a 1:4 rights issue at ₹200. A shareholder with 400 shares is entitled to 100 new shares. TERP = (4 × ₹300 + 1 × ₹200) ÷ 5 = ₹280. If she subscribes, she pays ₹20,000 and holds 500 shares worth ₹1,40,000 — the same as her earlier ₹1,20,000 plus ₹20,000 paid. If she ignores the offer, her 400 shares fall to about ₹1,12,000.
faqs: What happens if I don't apply in a rights issue?

Your rights entitlements lapse at the end of the issue, and you do not get the new shares. Because the market price typically adjusts downward toward the theoretical ex-rights price, your holding loses some value relative to before. Selling the REs during the renunciation period lets you capture their market value instead.
Can I apply for more shares than my entitlement?

In many rights issues, shareholders may apply for additional shares beyond their entitlement. Additional shares are allotted only if some shareholders do not subscribe, and the basis of allotment is given in the letter of offer. Promoters often also commit to subscribe to unsubscribed portions.

items.title: Bonus Shares Meaning: Bonus Issue Ratio and Price Adjustment
items.description: What a bonus issue is, how bonus ratios like 1:1 and 1:2 work, why the share price falls after the ex-date and how bonus shares differ from a stock split.
items.short: A bonus issue is a free distribution of additional shares to existing shareholders by converting part of the company's reserves into share capital.
body: When a company capitalises its free reserves, securities premium or capital redemption reserve, it issues new fully paid shares to shareholders in a stated ratio. A 1:1 bonus gives one new share for every share held; 1:2 gives one new share for every two held. No money is paid by shareholders and none is raised by the company. Bonus shares cannot be issued from revaluation reserves or in lieu of dividend.

Since the company's total value does not change, the share price adjusts on the ex-date roughly in proportion to the ratio. If you held 100 shares at ₹900 before a 1:2 bonus, you hold 150 shares worth about ₹600 each afterward — still about ₹90,000. Exchanges also adjust derivative contracts so that futures and options positions remain economically the same.

Why issue bonus shares then? It brings the share price into a more affordable range, increases the number of shares available for trading, signals management confidence that reserves are healthy, and moves reserves into paid-up capital. Dividend per share may fall but total dividend paid may stay the same or rise.

Bonus vs stock split is a classic exam question. A bonus changes the balance sheet — reserves fall and share capital rises — while the face value per share stays the same. A split changes the face value (for example ₹10 to ₹2) and leaves reserves and total share capital unchanged.
items.example: A company has 10 crore shares of face value ₹10 (share capital ₹100 crore) and reserves of ₹800 crore. It announces a 1:1 bonus. After the issue it has 20 crore shares, share capital of ₹200 crore and reserves of ₹700 crore — total net worth unchanged at ₹900 crore. An investor's 60 shares at ₹1,480 become 120 shares at roughly ₹740.
faqs: Are bonus shares really free?

In the sense that you pay nothing, yes. But your wealth does not increase at the moment of issue because the share price adjusts downward in proportion. The value of your holding before and after the ex-date is about the same; any gain or loss afterwards comes from normal market movement.
How long does it take to receive bonus shares?

Bonus shares are credited to demat accounts by the depositories after the record date, and SEBI has shortened the timeline so that bonus shares become available for trading soon after the record date. Check the company's exchange announcement for the exact credit and trading dates for any specific bonus issue.

items.title: Stock Split Meaning: Face Value Change and Price Effect
items.description: Stock split explained with an Indian example: how cutting face value from ₹10 to ₹2 multiplies shares and lowers the price without changing holding value.
items.short: A stock split divides each existing share into several shares of a lower face value, increasing the number of shares without changing the company's total capital.
body: In a split, a company with shares of face value ₹10 may split each into five shares of ₹2, or ten shares of ₹1. The share count multiplies, the face value falls by the same factor, and the market price adjusts proportionately on the ex-date. Total paid-up capital and reserves on the balance sheet are unaffected; only the denomination of shares changes.

Companies split shares mainly to improve liquidity and affordability. A share trading at ₹12,000 can feel out of reach for small investors and leads to wide bid-ask spreads. After a 1:10 split, the price is around ₹1,200, and more participants can buy in smaller amounts.

A split requires board and shareholder approval because it alters the memorandum's capital clause. A record date is fixed, and depositories credit the new shares under a new ISIN after the old ISIN is cancelled. Exchanges adjust open futures and options contracts — the strike price is divided and the lot size multiplied — so that the position value stays the same.

The reverse of a split is a consolidation (reverse split), which combines shares into fewer shares of higher face value; it is rare in India. People often think a split makes a share 'cheap'. Valuation ratios like price-to-earnings do not change because earnings per share fall by the same factor as price.
items.example: An investor holds 30 shares of face value ₹10 trading at ₹4,500 (₹1,35,000). The company splits each share into 5 of face value ₹2. After the ex-date, she holds 150 shares, and the price is about ₹900 — still ₹1,35,000. EPS of ₹150 becomes ₹30, so the P/E stays at 30. A call option with strike ₹4,600 becomes strike ₹920, with the lot size five times larger.
faqs: Is a stock split good for shareholders?

A split by itself does not create value; it only changes the number of shares and price per share. It can improve liquidity and widen the investor base, which some studies associate with short-term interest, but long-term returns depend on the company's business performance, not on the split.
What is the difference between a stock split and a bonus issue?

A split reduces face value and keeps reserves unchanged; a bonus keeps face value the same and converts reserves into share capital. In both cases the number of shares rises and the price adjusts, so the investor's holding value is unaffected at the time of the action.

items.title: QIP Meaning: Qualified Institutions Placement Explained
items.description: What a QIP is, why listed Indian companies use it to raise money quickly, the SEBI floor price formula, allottee limits and how it differs from an FPO.
items.short: A qualified institutions placement is a fund-raising route in which a listed company issues shares or convertible securities only to qualified institutional buyers.
body: SEBI introduced the QIP route in 2006 so Indian listed companies could raise capital from domestic institutions quickly, instead of going abroad through depository receipts. A QIP needs shareholder approval by special resolution, but unlike an FPO it does not require a full offer document to be reviewed by SEBI — a placement document is prepared and filed with the exchanges.

Pricing follows a formula in the ICDR Regulations. The floor price is the average of the weekly high and low closing prices over the two weeks before the 'relevant date' (the date the board or committee decides to open the issue). The issuer may offer a discount of up to 5% on this floor price with shareholder approval.

Allotment rules ensure the issue is genuinely spread among institutions: at least 10% must go to mutual funds where available, a minimum number of allottees is required depending on issue size, and no single allottee can receive more than 50% of the issue. Promoters and their related parties cannot participate.

QIPs are popular with banks, NBFCs and growth companies because they can be launched and closed within days. The downside for existing retail shareholders is dilution without the chance to participate, unlike a rights issue.
items.example: On the relevant date, a bank's two-week average of weekly high and low closing prices is ₹520. The floor price is ₹520; with a 5% discount, the issue price can be as low as ₹494. Raising ₹3,000 crore at ₹494 means issuing about 6.07 crore new shares. If the bank had 150 crore shares, the dilution is about 3.9%.
faqs: Can retail investors take part in a QIP?

No. A QIP is restricted to qualified institutional buyers such as mutual funds, insurers, banks and eligible foreign portfolio investors. Retail investors can buy the shares afterwards in the secondary market once they are listed, but they cannot apply in the placement itself.
What is the difference between a QIP and an FPO?

An FPO is a public offer open to all categories of investors and requires a full offer document. A QIP is a private placement to QIBs only, uses a shorter placement document and is priced using SEBI's formula. QIPs are faster and cheaper, which is why listed companies prefer them.

items.title: Share Buyback Meaning: Tender Offer, Limits and Example
items.description: Buyback of shares explained: why companies repurchase shares, the tender offer route, acceptance ratio, small shareholder reservation and SEBI limits.
items.short: A share buyback is when a company repurchases its own shares from existing shareholders, reducing the number of shares outstanding and returning cash to investors.
body: Buybacks are governed by Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013 and the SEBI (Buy-Back of Securities) Regulations, 2018. A company may buy back up to 25% of its paid-up capital and free reserves, with a lower limit of 10% if approved only by the board. After the buyback, its debt-to-equity ratio must generally not exceed 2:1. Bought-back shares are extinguished.

The tender offer route is now the main method: the company announces a buyback price, usually at a premium to the market, and a record date. Shareholders tender shares through the exchange's window. SEBI has phased out the open market route through stock exchanges. In a tender offer, 15% of the buyback is reserved for small shareholders — those holding shares worth up to ₹2 lakh on the record date.

If more shares are tendered than the company wants to buy, acceptance is proportionate. The acceptance ratio for small shareholders is often higher than for others because their reserved quota is smaller relative to their total holding. Unaccepted shares are returned to the shareholder's demat account.

Companies use buybacks to return surplus cash, signal that management sees the share as undervalued, and improve earnings per share. Investors sometimes assume they will sell all their shares at the premium price — in reality only a fraction is usually accepted, and the remaining shares trade at the market price. Tax treatment of buyback proceeds has changed in recent years, so check the current income-tax rules.
items.example: A company announces a tender buyback of 1 crore shares at ₹1,500 when the market price is ₹1,300. The small-shareholder quota is 15 lakh shares. If small shareholders tender 50 lakh eligible shares, their acceptance ratio is 30%. A small investor with 100 shares has 30 accepted at ₹1,500 (₹45,000) and gets 70 shares back.
faqs: Is a buyback compulsory for shareholders?

No. Participation is voluntary. Shareholders who do not tender keep their shares and end up with a slightly higher percentage ownership because the total number of shares falls. Whether to tender depends on the premium offered, expected acceptance ratio and one's own investment view.
Who counts as a small shareholder in a buyback?

Under SEBI's buyback regulations, a small shareholder is one whose holding is worth up to ₹2 lakh on the record date, based on the closing price on the exchange with the highest trading volume. Fifteen percent of the buyback, or their entitlement if higher, is reserved for this category.

items.title: Delisting of Shares: Meaning, Voluntary vs Compulsory
items.description: What delisting means for shareholders, how voluntary delisting by reverse book building works, the 90% threshold and what happens in compulsory delisting.
items.short: Delisting is the permanent removal of a company's shares from a stock exchange, after which they can no longer be traded on that exchange.
body: Delisting in India is governed by the SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021. There are two types. Voluntary delisting happens when the promoters choose to take the company private and buy out public shareholders. Compulsory delisting happens when an exchange removes a company as a penalty, for example for prolonged non-compliance, suspension or failure to pay listing fees.

In voluntary delisting, a floor price is calculated under SEBI's formula, and the traditional method is reverse book building: public shareholders offer their shares at prices they choose, and the discovered price is the one at which the acquirer's holding reaches 90% of total shares. The acquirer may accept that price or make a counter-offer. SEBI amendments in 2024 also allow a fixed-price route for certain companies at a premium over the floor price — check the current regulations for conditions.

If delisting succeeds, shareholders who did not tender can still sell to the promoters at the exit price for at least one year through an exit window. If it fails, shares tendered are returned and the company stays listed.

Compulsory delisting is harsher for investors: there is no buyer at a premium. Promoters must buy shares at a fair value fixed by an independent valuer, and the company, its whole-time directors and promoters are barred from accessing the securities market for ten years. Shareholders of delisted companies still own their shares but may find them very hard to sell.
items.example: A promoter holds 80% of a company with 10 crore shares and wants to delist. To cross 90%, at least 1 crore more shares (10% of total) must be acquired. In reverse book building, public shareholders bid between the floor price of ₹200 and higher prices. If the cumulative offer reaches 1 crore shares at ₹265, the discovered price is ₹265, and the acquirer must pay about ₹265 crore to complete the purchase at that price.
faqs: What happens to my shares if a company is delisted?

You still own them in your demat account. In voluntary delisting, you can tender during the offer or sell to the promoters at the exit price during the exit window. In compulsory delisting, promoters must buy at the fair value fixed by an independent valuer. After that, selling usually requires finding a private buyer.
Can a delisted company list again?

Yes, but after a waiting period. Under SEBI rules, a company that delisted voluntarily cannot reapply for listing for a specified number of years, and a compulsorily delisted company faces a longer bar. It must then follow the normal listing process, including a fresh offer document.

items.title: T+1 Settlement Meaning: How Indian Stock Trades Settle
items.description: T+1 settlement explained: when shares and money reach you after a trade in India, how settlement days are counted, holidays, and the optional T+0 cycle.
items.short: T+1 settlement means a stock trade done on trading day T is settled — shares delivered to the buyer and funds to the seller — on the next working day.
body: India moved in phases from T+2 to T+1 for all listed equity shares, completing the shift in January 2023, making it one of the first major markets on a T+1 cycle. 'T' is the trade date and '+1' counts settlement days, which exclude weekends and settlement holidays, not calendar days.

What happens in between: on T, the exchange sends trade details to the clearing corporation, which computes each broker's net obligation of funds and securities. On T+1 morning, brokers complete pay-in — sellers' shares are moved from their demat accounts and buyers' funds are paid to the clearing corporation. Pay-out follows the same day: shares go directly to buyers' demat accounts and funds to brokers, who credit sellers.

Shorter settlement reduces counterparty risk because fewer days of price movement are exposed, frees up capital faster for investors and reduces margin needs. SEBI also introduced an optional same-day (T+0) settlement cycle for a limited set of shares from 2024, running alongside T+1; its scope may expand, so check current SEBI circulars.

A common confusion is about selling shares bought the previous day (BTST). You can sell shares on T+1 before they are credited, but if your purchase fails because the seller short-delivers, your own sale can go into auction. Another confusion: intraday trades squared off the same day have no delivery obligation and only result in a money settlement.
items.example: Kiran buys 25 shares at ₹1,820 on Thursday. Funds of ₹45,500 plus charges are taken by her broker for pay-in on Friday (T+1), and the shares reach her demat account the same Friday. If she had instead traded on Friday, settlement would happen on Monday — Saturday and Sunday are not settlement days. If Monday is an exchange holiday, settlement moves to Tuesday.
faqs: Can I sell shares before they reach my demat account?

Yes. Shares bought on T can be sold on T+1 before they are credited (often called BTST). The risk is that if the original seller fails to deliver, your purchase goes to auction while you still owe delivery on your sale, which can lead to auction or close-out charges on your sale.
Is T+1 the same for derivatives?

No. Equity futures and options are settled daily through mark-to-market and at expiry in cash or, for stock derivatives, by physical delivery. Cash flows for daily mark-to-market settle on the next working day. The T+1 cycle described here applies to the equity cash (delivery) segment.

items.title: Clearing Corporation: Meaning and Role in Settlement
items.description: What a clearing corporation does: novation, netting of trades, margins, settlement guarantee fund and why it makes Indian exchange trades safe to settle.
items.short: A clearing corporation clears and settles trades executed on a stock exchange, acting as the legal counterparty to every buyer and seller so that settlement is guaranteed.
body: Each Indian exchange has a linked clearing corporation: NSE Clearing Ltd for NSE, Indian Clearing Corporation Ltd (ICCL) for BSE, and separate clearing corporations for commodity exchanges such as MCX. They are recognised and regulated by SEBI and are distinct companies from the exchanges themselves.

The key concept is novation. Once a trade is matched, the clearing corporation steps in between the parties: it becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer. Your trade is therefore not exposed to the default of the unknown person on the other side, only to the clearing corporation, which manages risk through margins and a Settlement Guarantee Fund (Core SGF).

Clearing involves netting all trades of each clearing member to work out how much money and how many shares they must deliver or receive. Settlement is the actual exchange of funds and securities through clearing banks and depositories. The clearing corporation also collects margins (SPAN, exposure, VaR, mark-to-market), monitors positions, and conducts auctions when sellers fail to deliver.

Because of interoperability between clearing corporations, a broker can clear trades executed on NSE and BSE through a single clearing corporation of its choice. Students sometimes confuse clearing members with trading members: a trading member executes trades; a clearing member settles them, either its own or those of other trading members.
items.example: A broker's clients buy 10,000 shares of a stock and sell 7,000 of the same stock on the same day. Instead of 17,000 separate deliveries, the clearing corporation nets them: the broker must receive 3,000 shares and pay the net amount. If a broker on the other side defaults on funds, the clearing corporation still completes the payout to the honest broker using the defaulter's margins and, if needed, the Core SGF.
faqs: What is novation in a clearing corporation?

Novation is the legal replacement of the original contract between buyer and seller with two new contracts: one between the buyer and the clearing corporation, and one between the seller and the clearing corporation. It gives each party a settlement guarantee and removes direct counterparty risk.
What is the Core Settlement Guarantee Fund?

It is a fund maintained by each clearing corporation to guarantee settlement of trades if a clearing member defaults and its own margins are not enough. It is built from contributions by the clearing corporation, the exchange and clearing members, with sizing based on stress tests prescribed by SEBI.

items.title: Pay-in and Pay-out in Stock Market Settlement Explained
items.description: Meaning of pay-in and pay-out in Indian stock settlement, what brokers and clients must deliver, direct payout of shares to demat and timelines for funds.
items.short: Pay-in is when clearing members deliver funds and securities to the clearing corporation; pay-out is when the clearing corporation releases them to the receiving members and clients.
body: Settlement has two legs. During pay-in, selling members deliver securities from clients' demat accounts to the clearing corporation's account at the depository, and buying members' clearing banks transfer the required funds. During pay-out, the clearing corporation credits the securities to buyers and the funds to sellers' members. Under T+1, both happen on the next working day after the trade.

SEBI has tightened how pay-out reaches clients. Securities are now paid out directly from the clearing corporation to the client's demat account rather than to a broker pool account, which reduced the risk of brokers misusing client shares. For funds, the broker must credit the client or keep the money in a running account settlement as per the client's choice and SEBI rules.

Sellers' shares are taken for pay-in using early pay-in or a DDPI or electronic authorisation given by the client. Buyers must have paid funds to their broker by the pay-in deadline; if not, the broker may square off or the shares may be held as unpaid securities and sold after a few days, as per SEBI rules on unpaid securities.

A misconception is that pay-out reaching your broker means it has reached you. In the funds leg, there can be a short gap while the broker processes payouts to your bank, and many brokers settle client funds periodically under the running account system unless you choose otherwise.
items.example: On Monday, Arjun sells 200 shares at ₹350 and Neha buys 200 shares at ₹350 through different brokers. On Tuesday morning, Arjun's broker delivers the 200 shares (pay-in of securities) and Neha's broker's clearing bank pays ₹70,000 (pay-in of funds). After processing, the clearing corporation credits the 200 shares directly into Neha's demat account and releases ₹70,000 to Arjun's broker (pay-out), which credits Arjun's ledger.
faqs: What is early pay-in?

Early pay-in means the seller's shares are delivered to the clearing corporation before the normal pay-in deadline, often on trade day itself when the client sells holdings. It helps brokers avoid collecting margins on the sale, because the delivery obligation is already met, and reduces the risk of short delivery.
What is a running account settlement?

It is an arrangement where a broker keeps client funds in a running account and settles them periodically — monthly or quarterly as the client chooses — rather than after every trade. SEBI requires brokers to actually settle these accounts on the scheduled dates and to return excess funds as per prescribed norms.

items.title: Short Delivery and Auction in Shares: Meaning and Cost
items.description: What happens when a seller fails to deliver shares: short delivery, the exchange auction, close-out price rules and the cost borne by the defaulting seller.
items.short: Short delivery occurs when a seller fails to deliver shares on settlement day; the clearing corporation then buys them in an auction or closes out the trade in cash at the seller's cost.
body: Short delivery usually happens when someone sells shares they do not have — for example, selling in delivery mode by mistake, selling BTST shares whose purchase itself failed, or not authorising the debit of shares from their demat account in time. In India, retail investors are not allowed to short sell in the cash market overnight, so any undelivered quantity is treated as a delivery default.

The clearing corporation conducts an auction to buy the shortfall from other sellers in the market. The buyer receives the auctioned shares a day later than normal. The defaulting seller pays the difference if the auction price is higher than the original sale price, plus penalties prescribed by the exchange.

If no shares are offered in the auction, the trade is closed out in cash. The close-out price, under exchange rules, is generally the higher of the highest price traded from trade day to auction day and a set percentage (commonly 20%) above the closing price on the auction day — check the exchange's current circular. This can be very costly for the seller.

Buyers sometimes think short delivery means they have lost money. In fact, the buyer either receives the shares through the auction or receives cash at the close-out price, which is usually above the buy price. The buyer does lose the shares they intended to hold, which matters if a corporate action such as a dividend or bonus record date was close.
items.example: Rahul sells 100 shares at ₹500 on Monday but delivers only 60 because 40 were pledged. On Tuesday, the clearing corporation auctions the 40 shares and buys them at ₹520. Rahul bears the ₹20 × 40 = ₹800 difference plus penalty. Had nobody offered shares and the close-out price been ₹612 (20% above a ₹510 closing price), Rahul's loss would be (₹612 − ₹500) × 40 = ₹4,480 plus penalty.
faqs: Can a retail investor short sell shares in India?

Retail investors can short sell in the equity cash segment only intraday, closing the position the same day. Overnight short positions in the cash market lead to short delivery and auction. To hold a short position longer, investors use stock futures, put options or the securities lending and borrowing (SLB) mechanism.
Who receives the money if a trade is closed out?

The buyer whose shares were short-delivered receives the close-out amount, credited by the clearing corporation through their broker. This amount is usually higher than the original purchase price because of the close-out price formula, which is meant to compensate the buyer and discourage sellers from defaulting.

items.title: Circuit Breaker in Stock Market: 10%, 15%, 20% Trading Halts
items.description: Market-wide circuit breaker explained: how Sensex or Nifty falls of 10%, 15% and 20% trigger trading halts in India, halt timings and the March 2020 example.
items.short: A market-wide circuit breaker is an automatic trading halt across all equity and equity-derivative markets when the Sensex or Nifty moves by 10%, 15% or 20% in a day.
body: SEBI's index-based circuit breaker applies to all exchanges together. It is triggered by the movement of either the BSE Sensex or the NSE Nifty 50, whichever breaches the threshold first, and applies to both upward and downward moves. The point levels are calculated from the index's previous closing value.

The halt duration depends on the threshold and the time of the day. For a 10% move before 1:00 p.m., trading halts for 45 minutes; between 1:00 and 2:30 p.m., for 15 minutes; after 2:30 p.m., there is no halt. For 15%, the halt is 1 hour 45 minutes before 1:00 p.m., 45 minutes between 1:00 and 2:00 p.m., and for the rest of the day after 2:00 p.m. A 20% move at any time halts trading for the rest of the day. After a halt, trading resumes with a pre-open call auction session.

The purpose is to give investors time to absorb information, check margins and avoid panic selling. It is different from the price band on individual stocks: a stock can hit its upper or lower band ('upper circuit' or 'lower circuit') while the overall market trades normally.

India's most-cited example is March 2020, when the market-wide circuit breaker was triggered twice in a single month during the pandemic sell-off. Many investors use 'circuit' loosely for both concepts; in exams, be precise about whether the question is about index-based halts or scrip-level bands.
items.example: The Nifty closed at 24,000 yesterday. A 10% fall means 21,600 (2,400 points). If the Nifty touches 21,600 at 11:20 a.m., all equity and equity-derivative trading on NSE and BSE halts for 45 minutes, followed by a 15-minute pre-open session. Had the Sensex crossed its 10% level first, the same halt would apply. A further fall to 20,400 (15%) after trading resumes, but still before 1:00 p.m., would trigger a 1-hour-45-minute halt.
faqs: Is a circuit breaker the same as upper circuit or lower circuit?

Not quite. 'Upper circuit' and 'lower circuit' describe a single stock hitting its daily price band, after which trades can occur only within the band. The market-wide circuit breaker is index-based and halts all trading on all exchanges. The two mechanisms work independently.
Do circuit breakers apply to currency and commodity markets?

The index-based market-wide circuit breaker described here applies to equity and equity derivative segments. Commodity and currency derivatives have their own daily price limits and margin rules set by the exchanges, which can include temporary cooling-off periods when limits are hit.

items.title: Price Band Meaning: Upper and Lower Circuit for Stocks
items.description: What a price band on a stock means, the 2%, 5%, 10% and 20% bands, why F&O stocks have no fixed band but dynamic limits, and why traders can get stuck.
items.short: A price band is the maximum percentage a stock's price can rise or fall in a single trading day from its previous close, as set by the exchange.
body: Exchanges assign each stock a daily price band, commonly 2%, 5%, 10% or 20%, based on factors like volatility, liquidity and surveillance concerns. Orders priced outside the band are rejected. When a stock reaches the top of its band, it is said to hit the 'upper circuit'; at the bottom, the 'lower circuit'. Trading continues within the band, but at the limit price there may be only buyers or only sellers.

Stocks with derivatives contracts (F&O stocks) do not have a fixed daily price band. Instead, exchanges apply dynamic price bands (operating ranges), typically starting at 10% and relaxed in steps if the market moves toward the edge. This allows price discovery in highly traded stocks while still preventing wild erroneous trades.

Price bands are also a surveillance tool. Exchanges can tighten a stock's band, for example from 20% to 5% or 2%, if it shows abnormal movements or comes under additional surveillance measures (ASM/GSM). Newly listed IPO shares have special pre-open sessions and bands on listing day.

The risk for investors is liquidity. If a small-cap stock is at a 5% lower circuit with a large pile of sell orders and no buyers, you may be unable to exit for several days in a row. Seeing a stock 'locked' in upper circuit is not a sign of strength by itself; it can also reflect thin trading or manipulation.
items.example: A stock closed at ₹240 and has a 5% price band. Today, orders can be placed only between ₹228 and ₹252. A buy order at ₹253 is rejected. If heavy buying pushes the price to ₹252, the stock is at upper circuit and buy orders pile up at ₹252 waiting for sellers. Tomorrow's band is calculated on the new closing price: if it closes at ₹252, tomorrow's range becomes ₹239.40–₹264.60.
faqs: Why do F&O stocks not have a price band?

Stocks in the derivatives segment are usually large and liquid, and fixed bands would distort arbitrage between the cash and futures markets. Instead, exchanges apply dynamic price bands that can be widened during the day in a controlled way. This still blocks erroneous orders while allowing genuine price discovery.
Can I sell a stock stuck at lower circuit?

You can place a sell order at the lower band price, but it will execute only if a buyer is willing to buy at that price. If sell orders far exceed buy orders, many sellers remain unfilled. This is why stocks with frequent circuit hits carry high liquidity risk.

items.title: Free-Float Market Cap Meaning: How Nifty Weights Stocks
items.description: Free-float market capitalisation explained: which shares are excluded, how free-float factors work and why Sensex and Nifty weights depend on this measure.
items.short: Free-float market capitalisation is the market value of only those shares readily available for trading, excluding promoter, strategic and locked-in holdings.
body: Full market capitalisation equals the share price multiplied by all outstanding shares. But in Indian companies, promoters often hold 50–75% of shares, and governments hold large stakes in PSUs. These shares rarely trade. Free-float market capitalisation multiplies the price by only the shares held by the public that can actually be bought and sold.

Index providers calculate an investable weight factor (IWF), or free-float factor, for each company. Shares held by promoters and promoter group, government in a strategic capacity, associate companies, employee welfare trusts and certain locked-in holdings are excluded. A company with 60% promoter holding has a free-float factor of about 0.40.

The Nifty 50, Sensex and most other Indian indices use free-float market capitalisation weighting. This means a company's influence on the index depends on how much of its stock is in public hands, not just its size. Index funds and ETFs tracking these indices therefore buy shares in proportion to free-float, matching what is actually available.

A common confusion is between free-float and minimum public shareholding. SEBI requires listed companies to maintain at least 25% public shareholding (with time allowed for new listings), but free-float for index purposes may differ because some 'public' holders, such as strategic investors, are also excluded.
items.example: Company A has 200 crore shares at ₹500, giving a full market cap of ₹1,00,000 crore. Promoters hold 72%, so the free-float factor is 0.28 and free-float market cap is ₹28,000 crore. Company B has a full market cap of ₹60,000 crore with only 20% promoter holding, so its free-float cap is ₹48,000 crore. Despite being smaller, B gets the larger weight in a free-float weighted index.
faqs: Why do indices use free-float instead of full market cap?

Free-float weighting reflects what investors can actually buy. A company with a large promoter stake would otherwise get an oversized weight, and index funds would struggle to buy enough shares, pushing the price up artificially. Free-float weighting also makes the index a fairer measure of public investors' experience.
Does free-float change over time?

Yes. When promoters sell shares through an OFS, a company issues new shares to the public, or locked-in shares become free, the free-float factor changes. Index providers update these factors periodically, usually during scheduled index reviews, and the change can lead to buying or selling by index funds.

items.title: Stock Market Index Meaning: Sensex vs Nifty Explained
items.description: What a stock market index is, how Sensex and Nifty 50 are built and calculated, base values, sectoral and broad indices, and how indices are used in practice.
items.short: A stock market index is a number that tracks the combined price movement of a selected group of stocks, representing the market or a segment of it.
body: India's two headline indices are the BSE Sensex, with 30 large companies and a base value of 100 for 1978–79, and the NSE Nifty 50, with 50 companies and a base value of 1,000 as of November 1995. Both are free-float market capitalisation weighted, so bigger companies with more publicly held shares move the index more.

The index value is calculated as the current free-float market capitalisation of the constituents divided by a divisor, which is adjusted for corporate actions and constituent changes so that the index level is continuous.
