A bonus issue or stock split therefore does not cause the index to jump. Index committees review constituents periodically, based on criteria such as free-float market cap, liquidity (often measured by impact cost) and listing history.

Beyond headline indices there are broad indices (Nifty 500, BSE 500), size-based indices (Midcap, Smallcap), sectoral indices (Bank Nifty, Nifty IT) and thematic or strategy indices. Indices serve as benchmarks for mutual funds, underlying assets for index futures and options, and a basis for ETFs and index funds.

Points versus percentage is a classic confusion. A 500-point fall in the Sensex sounds dramatic, but when the index is around 80,000 it is only about 0.6%. Also, the index going up does not mean every stock went up — a handful of heavyweights can move it while most stocks fall.
items.example: An index has a base market cap of ₹5,00,000 crore set equal to 1,000 points, so the divisor is 500. Today, the free-float market cap of constituents is ₹12,40,000 crore, giving an index value of 2,480. If a constituent issues bonus shares, its price falls but the share count rises, so the market cap — and the index — stay unchanged without any divisor adjustment.
faqs: What is the difference between Sensex and Nifty?

The Sensex belongs to BSE and has 30 stocks with a 1978–79 base; the Nifty 50 belongs to NSE Indices and has 50 stocks with a 1995 base. Both use free-float methodology and move broadly together. The Nifty is more widely used as the underlying for derivatives and index funds.
Can I invest directly in an index?

No, an index is just a number. You can get index exposure through index funds and ETFs that hold the constituent stocks in proportion to their weights, or through index futures and options, which are derivatives. Each route carries its own costs, tracking differences and risks.

items.title: Limit Order vs Market Order: Meaning with Examples
items.description: Difference between a limit order and a market order in the Indian stock market, when each executes, the risk of slippage and how order validity works.
items.short: A market order buys or sells immediately at the best available price, while a limit order executes only at a specified price or better.
body: A market order prioritises execution over price. It matches against the best opposite orders in the book, and if the quantity at the best price is not enough, it moves to the next price levels. This can lead to slippage in illiquid stocks or during volatile moments — the average price may be worse than the last traded price you saw.

A limit order prioritises price over execution. A buy limit at ₹250 will execute at ₹250 or lower; a sell limit at ₹250 at ₹250 or higher. If the market never reaches your price, the order sits in the order book unexecuted until it expires or you cancel it. Partial execution is possible if only part of your quantity can be matched at your price.

Orders also carry a validity condition. A DAY order stays active until the end of the trading session; an IOC (immediate or cancel) order executes whatever quantity is possible immediately and cancels the rest. Many brokers also offer after-market orders, which are placed when the market is closed and sent to the exchange at the next session's open.

Beginners often assume a market order fills at the price on their screen. In thinly traded stocks the screen may show a last traded price from several minutes ago. Using limit orders is a practical way to control cost; market orders make sense mainly in highly liquid stocks where the bid-ask spread is tiny.
items.example: The order book shows sellers: 100 shares at ₹420.00, 150 at ₹420.50, 300 at ₹422.00. A market buy for 400 shares fills 100 at ₹420, 150 at ₹420.50 and 150 at ₹422, for an average of (42,000 + 63,075 + 63,300) ÷ 400 = ₹420.94. A limit buy at ₹420.50 for 400 shares would fill only 250 shares and leave 150 waiting in the book.
faqs: Is a market order executed at the last traded price?

Not necessarily. A market order executes against the best available opposite orders at that moment. If those orders are at a different price from the last trade, or if your quantity is larger than what is available at the best price, your average price will differ from the last traded price.
What is an IOC order?

Immediate or cancel (IOC) is a validity condition. The order tries to execute as much quantity as possible as soon as it reaches the exchange, and any unexecuted part is cancelled immediately instead of waiting in the order book. It is useful when you want to avoid leaving orders hanging.

items.title: Stop-Loss Order Meaning: Trigger Price, SL vs SL-M
items.description: How a stop-loss order works in the Indian stock market, trigger price versus limit price, SL and SL-M orders, and why a stop-loss may not always execute.
items.short: A stop-loss order is an instruction to buy or sell once the price reaches a specified trigger price, used to limit losses or protect profits.
body: A stop-loss order has a trigger price. Until the market reaches the trigger, the order is held without being active in the order book. Once the last traded price touches the trigger, the order is released to the exchange. For a long position, a sell stop-loss trigger is placed below the current price; for a short position, a buy stop-loss is placed above it.

There are two common variants. A stop-loss limit (SL) order has both a trigger price and a limit price: once triggered, it becomes a limit order at the limit price. A stop-loss market (SL-M) order becomes a market order when triggered. Some brokers and segments restrict SL-M orders, so check what your platform allows.

The trade-off is execution certainty versus price certainty. An SL order protects you from selling far below your limit, but in a fast fall the price can skip past your limit and leave the order unexecuted. An SL-M order will execute, but possibly at a much worse price, especially when a stock gaps down at the open after bad news.

Stop-losses are risk management tools, not guarantees. They do not protect against gap openings, and placing them too close to the current price can lead to being stopped out by normal fluctuations. In exams, remember: trigger price activates; limit price controls the execution price.
items.example: Sneha bought 200 shares at ₹600. She places a sell SL order with trigger ₹570 and limit ₹568. If the price drifts down to ₹570, the order activates and sells at ₹568 or better, limiting her loss to about ₹32 × 200 = ₹6,400. If results disappoint and the stock opens at ₹540, the limit of ₹568 is above the market, so the order stays unexecuted and her paper loss is ₹12,000.
faqs: What is the difference between trigger price and limit price?

The trigger price is the level that activates the stop-loss order. The limit price is the worst price at which you are willing to trade once activated. For a sell stop-loss, the limit is usually set slightly below the trigger to allow some room for execution in a falling market.
Does a stop-loss order guarantee my maximum loss?

No. A stop-loss limit order may remain unexecuted if the price falls past your limit, and a stop-loss market order may execute well below the trigger in a gap-down or fast-moving market. It helps manage risk in normal conditions but cannot remove gap or liquidity risk.

items.title: Bid-Ask Spread Meaning: How to Read the Order Book
items.description: What the bid-ask spread is, how to read the best bid and best ask in an Indian order book, why spreads widen in illiquid stocks and how it affects your cost.
items.short: The bid-ask spread is the difference between the highest price a buyer is willing to pay (bid) and the lowest price a seller is willing to accept (ask).
body: Every trading screen shows a market depth or order book. The best bid is the top buy order; the best ask (or offer) is the top sell order. A trade happens only when someone accepts the other side's price. The gap between the two is the spread, often expressed in rupees or as a percentage of the mid-price.

Spreads are a hidden transaction cost. If you buy at the ask and immediately sell at the bid, you lose the spread even if the 'price' has not moved. In highly liquid large-cap stocks, the spread may be just one tick (₹0.05 or ₹0.10). In small, rarely traded stocks, it can be 1–2% or more, which matters a lot for short-term traders.

Market makers and active traders earn by capturing the spread — buying at the bid and selling at the ask. Exchanges watch spreads as a liquidity measure, and index providers use the related concept of impact cost when selecting constituents.

A misconception is that the last traded price (LTP) is the price you can trade at. The LTP is history; what you can actually buy at is the best ask, and sell at is the best bid. Also note that the visible depth shows only the top few levels, and large orders may consume several levels.
items.example: A stock's order book shows best bid ₹184.20 (500 shares) and best ask ₹184.80 (300 shares). The spread is ₹0.60. The mid-price is ₹184.50, so the spread is 0.60 ÷ 184.50 ≈ 0.33%. A trader who buys 300 shares at ₹184.80 and immediately sells them at ₹184.20 loses ₹180 before any brokerage or taxes, even though nothing has changed in the stock.
faqs: Why is the spread wider in small-cap stocks?

Fewer buyers and sellers place orders, so the best bid and ask are further apart. Market participants also demand a larger margin for the risk of holding a less liquid stock. Wider spreads mean higher hidden costs, which is why limit orders are especially useful in such stocks.
Does the bid-ask spread apply to options too?

Yes, and often more sharply. Far out-of-the-money or illiquid option strikes can have spreads that are a large percentage of the premium. Option traders check the spread and open interest before trading, because entering and exiting can cost more than expected.

items.title: Impact Cost Meaning: Formula and Example for Liquidity
items.description: Impact cost explained with a worked example: how it measures liquidity for an order size, the ideal price formula and why NSE uses it for index selection.
items.short: Impact cost is the percentage by which the actual execution price of an order of a given size differs from the ideal price, which is the mid-point of the best bid and ask.
body: Impact cost measures liquidity more precisely than the spread because it accounts for order size. A small order may fill at the best ask, but a large order eats into deeper levels of the order book at worse prices. The more the price is 'impacted', the less liquid the stock is for that order size.

The formula is: impact cost (%) = (actual execution price − ideal price) ÷ ideal price × 100, where ideal price = (best bid + best ask) ÷ 2. For a sell order, the difference is calculated with the ideal price above the execution price, and the result is still expressed as a positive cost.

NSE Indices uses impact cost as a liquidity screen when selecting stocks for indices such as the Nifty 50; a stock must show low impact cost for a specified basket size over a review period. Exact thresholds and basket sizes are set in the index methodology and are revised from time to time — check the latest NSE Indices document.

Impact cost is a snapshot that changes through the day. Institutional investors care about it the most, which is why they split large orders into smaller pieces or use block deal windows. For retail investors, it explains why the same stock can be cheap to trade in small sizes but costly for big orders.
items.example: Order book (sell side): 1,000 shares at ₹100.10, 2,000 at ₹100.20, 3,000 at ₹100.40. Best bid is ₹99.90, so the ideal price is (99.90 + 100.10) ÷ 2 = ₹100.00. Buying 3,000 shares fills 1,000 at ₹100.10 and 2,000 at ₹100.20, an average of ₹100.1667. Impact cost = (100.1667 − 100) ÷ 100 × 100 ≈ 0.17%. Buying 6,000 shares would average ₹100.2833, an impact cost of about 0.28%.
faqs: What is the ideal price in impact cost?

The ideal price is the average of the best bid and best ask at that moment. It represents the theoretical price at which a very small order could trade without moving the market. Impact cost measures how far a real order of a given size moves away from this price.
Is low impact cost good for investors?

Yes. A low impact cost means the stock is liquid enough that large orders can be executed without moving the price much. Index providers prefer such stocks because index funds and ETFs need to buy and sell them in bulk, and traders face lower hidden costs.

items.title: Record Date vs Ex-Date: Who Gets Dividend, Bonus or Split
items.description: Record date and ex-date explained for Indian shares under T+1: when to buy to get a dividend, bonus or split, and why the price falls on the ex-date.
items.short: The record date is the date on which a company checks its shareholder list for a corporate benefit; the ex-date is the first day the share trades without that benefit.
body: When a company declares a dividend, bonus, split or rights issue, it fixes a record date. Everyone whose name appears as a beneficial owner in the depository records at the end of that date is entitled. Because buying a share does not make you the owner until settlement, the exchange sets an ex-date — the date from which a buyer will not get the benefit.

With India's T+1 settlement, the ex-date and record date are now the same day. To be entitled, you must buy no later than the trading day before the record date, so that your purchase settles on or before the record date. A buyer on the ex-date (record date) itself does not qualify, because the purchase settles a day later.

On the ex-date, the share price adjusts for the value of the benefit. For a dividend, the price typically opens lower by about the dividend amount; for a bonus or split, it adjusts in proportion to the ratio. Exchanges also adjust strike prices and lot sizes of derivatives for large special dividends and for bonus, split and rights.

A frequent mistake is 'dividend stripping' — buying just before the record date to collect a dividend, assuming the price will not fall. In practice the price adjusts, and taxes on the dividend can make the trade a loss. Another error is using the pre-T+1 rule that the ex-date is one day before the record date; that rule is outdated.
items.example: A company declares a ₹20 dividend with record date Friday, 14 March. Since ex-date equals record date under T+1, buying on Thursday the 13th (settles Friday) qualifies; buying on Friday does not. If the share closes at ₹860 on Thursday, it is likely to open near ₹840 on Friday. An investor with 150 shares receives ₹3,000 in dividend, subject to tax deducted at source if applicable.
faqs: If I sell on the ex-date, do I still get the dividend?

Yes. If you held the shares before the ex-date and sell on the ex-date or later, your sale settles after the record date, so you are still on the register on the record date and receive the benefit. The buyer of your shares on the ex-date does not get it.
What is book closure?

Book closure is an older method where the company closes its register of members for a period to determine entitlements. With depositories maintaining electronic records, listed companies mostly use a single record date instead. Some still mention book closure periods, especially for annual general meeting dividends.

items.title: Corporate Actions Meaning: Dividend, Bonus, Split, Rights
items.description: What corporate actions are, the main types in Indian markets such as dividend, bonus, split, rights, buyback and merger, and how they reach your demat.
items.short: Corporate actions are events initiated by a listed company that change its securities or deliver benefits to shareholders, such as dividends, bonus issues, splits, rights and buybacks.
body: Corporate actions fall into three broad groups. Mandatory actions apply to all shareholders automatically — cash dividends, bonus issues, stock splits, consolidations and mergers or demergers that allot new shares. Voluntary actions need the shareholder to choose — buyback tenders, open offers, rights issues. Mandatory-with-choice actions give a default with an option, such as some dividend reinvestment choices.

Each action goes through board approval, shareholder approval where required, an announcement to the exchanges and fixation of a record date. The registrar and transfer agent (RTA) prepares the entitlement list from depository data, and the depositories credit new securities to demat accounts. Cash benefits go to the bank account linked with the demat.

Exchanges and clearing corporations adjust prices, indices and derivative contracts after corporate actions so that positions remain fair. For example, after a 1:1 bonus, futures prices and option strikes are halved and lot sizes doubled. Index divisors are changed after mergers or spin-offs.

Investors often miss voluntary actions because they need active participation. Ignoring a rights issue or a buyback tender is a choice too, with consequences for value and ownership percentage. Keeping your demat contact details, bank account and email updated is the simplest way to avoid missing notices.
items.example: In one year, an investor holding 200 shares of a company sees: a ₹12 dividend (₹2,400 credited to her bank), a 1:1 bonus (holding becomes 400 shares), and a demerger in which one share of a new company is given for every four held (100 shares of the new company credited). She also receives a buyback offer, which she must actively tender if she wants to participate — the other three happened automatically.
faqs: Do corporate actions affect futures and options positions?

Yes. For bonus, split, rights and large special dividends, exchanges adjust strike prices, lot sizes or both so that the value of open positions remains the same before and after the event. Ordinary dividends usually do not lead to adjustment, which is why they are priced into futures.
Who handles corporate actions for a company?

The company's board decides on the action, and its registrar and transfer agent (RTA) handles the processing, coordinating with depositories, exchanges and banks. Investors resolve issues such as unpaid dividends or missing credits by contacting the RTA or the company's investor relations team.

items.title: Contract Note Meaning: What It Shows and Why It Matters
items.description: What a contract note is, the details and charges it shows (brokerage, STT, GST, stamp duty), when brokers must send it and how to use it to check trades.
items.short: A contract note is the legal confirmation a stock broker issues to a client for trades executed on an exchange, showing prices, quantities and all charges.
body: SEBI and the exchanges require brokers to issue a contract note for every trading day on which the client trades, generally within 24 hours of execution. Most brokers send it electronically, digitally signed, to the client's registered email. It is the primary evidence of your trades if there is ever a dispute.

A contract note shows the order number, trade number, time, exchange and segment, the security, quantity, price, and whether it was a buy or sell. It also shows each charge separately: brokerage, securities transaction tax (STT), exchange transaction charges, SEBI turnover fees, stamp duty, and GST on brokerage and charges. It carries the client's unique client code (UCC) and PAN.

Checking contract notes helps you spot unauthorised trades, wrong quantities and excessive charges. If you see a trade you did not place, you should raise it with the broker immediately and escalate to the exchange if unresolved. Exchanges also send trade alerts by SMS and email directly to clients, which you can cross-check with the contract note.

Contract notes are important for tax as well. They support capital gains calculations and show STT paid. Investors sometimes rely only on the broker's P&L report; keeping contract notes (or downloading them periodically) is the safer practice.
items.example: Mohan buys 100 shares at ₹1,000 (value ₹1,00,000). His contract note shows illustrative charges: brokerage ₹20, STT ₹100 (0.1% on delivery buy), exchange charges ₹3, stamp duty ₹15, SEBI fee ₹0.10 and GST of 18% on brokerage, exchange charges and SEBI fee (about ₹4.16). Total cost ≈ ₹1,00,142. Rates change — check current exchange and tax notifications rather than these figures.
faqs: What should I do if my contract note shows a trade I did not place?

Write to the broker immediately with details, ask for the order log and call recording, and keep records. If the broker does not resolve it, file a complaint with the exchange or through SEBI SCORES, and if needed use the online dispute resolution (ODR) mechanism. Prompt action strengthens your case.
Is a contract note required for mutual fund purchases?

Contract notes are issued for trades executed on stock exchanges, including ETFs and mutual fund units bought through exchange platforms. Direct mutual fund purchases with an AMC generate an account statement instead, such as the consolidated account statement, rather than a contract note.

items.title: DDPI Meaning: Demat Debit and Pledge Instruction vs POA
items.description: What DDPI is, why SEBI introduced it to replace the broad power of attorney, the limited purposes it covers and how selling works if you don't sign it.
items.short: DDPI is a limited authorisation a client gives to a broker-DP to debit or pledge securities from the client's demat account only for specified purposes.
body: Earlier, brokers took a general power of attorney (POA) from clients to move shares for settlement. Misuse of POAs — including pledging client shares for the broker's own borrowing — led SEBI to introduce the DDPI framework in 2022. The DDPI restricts what the broker can do with your holdings.

A DDPI covers four purposes: transfer of securities for delivery against your sale on the exchange; pledging or re-pledging in favour of the broker or clearing corporation for margin; mutual fund transactions executed on stock exchange order-entry platforms; and tendering shares in open offers or buybacks through the exchange. Anything else, such as an off-market transfer, still needs your separate authorisation.

Signing a DDPI is optional. Without it, you can still sell shares by authorising each sale electronically through the depository's e-DIS/TPIN or OTP process. The DDPI simply saves you this step every time you sell, which active traders find convenient.

A common misunderstanding is that DDPI lets the broker sell your shares. It does not authorise trades — only the delivery of shares you have already sold. Another point: shares pledged for margin under the DDPI remain in your demat account with a pledge marked, and you continue to get corporate benefits.
items.example: Lata has signed a DDPI with her broker. She sells 50 shares on Monday; on Tuesday the broker-DP debits the 50 shares and delivers them for pay-in without asking her for a TPIN. Her friend Raj has not signed a DDPI; when he sells, he gets a prompt to authorise the debit through CDSL or NSDL's e-DIS with an OTP. If Raj misses it, his sale may be short-delivered and go into auction.
faqs: Is DDPI mandatory to trade?

No. SEBI made DDPI optional. Clients can trade without it and authorise each delivery through the depository's electronic DIS process using a TPIN or OTP. Some brokers may require DDPI for certain products, such as pledging shares for margin, so check your broker's terms.
Can a broker transfer my shares off-market using DDPI?

No. A DDPI is limited to delivery against exchange sales, margin pledges, exchange-platform mutual fund transactions and tendering in buybacks or open offers. Off-market transfers or transfers to another person's account require separate instructions from you.

items.title: Margin Trading Facility (MTF) Meaning, Interest and Risks
items.description: How the margin trading facility works in India: part payment, broker funding, interest, pledge of shares, margin calls and the risks of leverage.
items.short: A margin trading facility lets an investor buy eligible shares by paying only part of the value upfront, with the stock broker funding the rest and charging interest.
body: MTF is offered by SEBI-registered brokers under exchange and SEBI rules. Only stocks in an eligible list (largely liquid Group I securities and certain ETFs) can be bought under MTF. The client pays the initial margin — at least the VaR and extreme loss margin required for that stock — and the broker lends the balance from its own funds or approved borrowings.

The purchased shares are pledged in favour of the broker as collateral, using a specific MTF pledge. The client pays interest on the funded amount for each day the position is held, at the rate set by the broker. If the share price falls and the client's margin falls below the required level, the broker issues a margin call; if it is not met, the broker can sell the shares.

Leverage cuts both ways. A small price rise produces a larger percentage gain on the client's own money, and a small fall produces a larger percentage loss — plus interest costs every day. Brokers must report MTF exposure to exchanges, and SEBI caps the broker's total MTF book relative to its net worth.

Many beginners confuse MTF with intraday leverage. Intraday positions must be closed the same day, while MTF lets you hold delivery positions for weeks or months. Another misconception is that MTF is free leverage; interest can quietly erode returns, especially if the position is held for long.
items.example: Sunil buys shares worth ₹2,00,000 under MTF, paying ₹50,000 margin; the broker funds ₹1,50,000 at an illustrative 15% per annum. After 60 days, interest ≈ ₹1,50,000 × 15% × 60/365 = ₹3,699. If the stock rises 10%, the gain of ₹20,000 minus interest leaves ₹16,301 — a 32.6% return on his ₹50,000. If it falls 10%, the loss of ₹20,000 plus interest is ₹23,699 — a 47.4% loss.
faqs: Which shares can be bought under MTF?

Only securities that appear in the exchanges' eligible list for margin trading, which is largely based on liquidity and trading frequency, plus some eligible ETFs. Brokers may restrict the list further. Shares outside this list must be bought with full payment.
What happens if I cannot meet a margin call in MTF?

If you do not add funds or collateral within the time given, the broker can sell some or all of the pledged shares to bring the account back within margin requirements. You bear any resulting loss and continue to owe any shortfall plus interest.

items.title: SLB Meaning: Securities Lending and Borrowing in India
items.description: How securities lending and borrowing works on Indian exchanges: lending shares for a fee, borrowing for short selling, tenure, corporate actions and risks.
items.short: Securities lending and borrowing (SLB) is an exchange-traded mechanism where shareholders lend their shares for a fee to borrowers, who must return them on a fixed date.
body: SLB in India runs on the stock exchange platform through approved intermediaries, with the clearing corporation acting as the counterparty to both sides. This guarantee is what makes it attractive: the lender does not depend on the borrower's creditworthiness, since the borrower must post margins with the clearing corporation.

Lenders are often long-term investors, mutual funds and insurers who earn an extra fee on idle holdings. Borrowers include traders who want to short sell beyond intraday, those who need shares to avoid short delivery, and arbitrageurs. Contracts can range from a day to twelve months, and borrowers can roll over or recall positions early under exchange rules.

Corporate actions are handled so that the lender is not disadvantaged. If a dividend is paid during the lending period, the borrower compensates the lender. For events such as bonus, split or rights, contracts are adjusted or foreclosed as per exchange rules. The lender, however, loses voting rights while the shares are lent.

The main misconception is that SLB transfers ownership permanently or exposes lenders to default risk. Ownership returns at the end of the contract, and the clearing corporation guarantees the return or cash compensation. Fees are market-driven and vary widely by stock and demand.
items.example: Ramesh holds 1,000 shares of a stock trading at ₹800 and lends them for 30 days at an annualised fee of 6%. His fee ≈ ₹8,00,000 × 6% × 30/365 = ₹3,945. A trader who expects the price to fall borrows these shares, sells them at ₹800 and buys back at ₹760 before returning them, earning ₹40,000 before the fee and costs. If the price rises, the trader loses instead.
faqs: Is lending shares through SLB safe?

The clearing corporation guarantees the transaction and holds margins from borrowers, so the lender's risk of not getting shares back is low. The lender still faces normal market risk on the shares and loses voting rights during the lending period. Fees and liquidity vary by stock.
Why would someone borrow shares instead of selling futures?

Some stocks have no futures contracts, and a borrower may need actual shares to meet a delivery obligation. SLB also allows short positions for a tenure that does not match futures expiry. Borrowing costs and availability decide which route is cheaper or practical.

items.title: RTA Meaning: Registrar and Share Transfer Agent's Role
items.description: What a registrar and share transfer agent does for companies and mutual funds, and its role in IPO allotment, transmission, dividends and service requests.
items.short: A registrar and share transfer agent (RTA) is a SEBI-registered intermediary that maintains shareholder or unitholder records and processes investor service requests for issuers.
body: RTAs are registered under the SEBI (Registrars to an Issue and Share Transfer Agents) Regulations, 1993. Companies and mutual funds appoint them to manage registers of holders, process transmission of securities on death, record nominations, distribute dividends and interest, handle demat and remat requests and respond to investor complaints.

In public issues, the registrar to an issue plays a central role. It collects application data from the bidding platform and SCSBs, rejects invalid applications (such as multiple applications with one PAN), finalises the basis of allotment with the exchange, credits shares to demat accounts and arranges unblocking of ASBA funds. IPO allotment status is checked on the registrar's website.

For mutual funds, RTAs such as CAMS and KFin Technologies maintain folio records, process purchases and redemptions, and generate account statements. For listed companies, RTAs coordinate with depositories for corporate action credits.

Investors often contact the company for issues that the RTA actually handles — such as unclaimed dividends, KYC updates for physical folios or transmission. Knowing that the RTA is the record-keeper speeds up resolution. RTAs must also follow SEBI's investor grievance timelines and are covered under the SCORES and ODR frameworks.
items.example: After an IPO closes on Wednesday, the registrar validates 25 lakh applications and finds 40,000 duplicates by PAN, which are rejected. On Thursday it finalises allotment with the designated exchange: the retail portion of 10 lakh lots is allotted by lottery among 18 lakh valid applicants. On Friday it instructs depositories to credit shares and SCSBs to debit allotted amounts and unblock the rest, so listing can happen on T+3.
faqs: Who should I contact for transmission of shares after a death?

For physical folios, contact the company's RTA, which processes transmission documents such as the death certificate and claim forms. For demat holdings, the surviving joint holder or nominee approaches the DP. Simplified documentation limits apply for smaller values under SEBI's norms.
How do I check IPO allotment status?

You can check on the registrar's website using your PAN, application number or DP ID, and also on the stock exchange websites. Your bank or UPI app will show whether the blocked amount was debited or released, which also indicates the allotment outcome.

items.title: Merchant Banker Meaning: Role in IPOs and Due Diligence
items.description: What a merchant banker does in India: managing IPOs and rights issues, due diligence, pricing, marketing, buybacks and open offers under SEBI regulations.
items.short: A merchant banker is a SEBI-registered intermediary that manages public issues and related corporate finance activities such as IPOs, rights issues, buybacks and open offers.
body: Merchant bankers are regulated under the SEBI (Merchant Bankers) Regulations. In an IPO they act as book running lead managers (BRLMs). They advise the company on issue structure and timing, carry out due diligence on the business and its disclosures, draft the offer document, coordinate with SEBI and exchanges, market the issue to investors and help discover the price.

Due diligence is their most important legal responsibility. The lead manager signs a due diligence certificate stating that the offer document is fair and adequate and complies with SEBI rules. SEBI can penalise merchant bankers for poor disclosure even after an issue is completed.

Beyond IPOs, merchant bankers manage rights issues, QIPs, offers for sale, buybacks, delisting offers and open offers under the takeover code, and may also underwrite issues. Many are divisions of large banks or brokerage groups.

People sometimes mix up merchant bankers with investment banks in the US or with commercial banks. In India, the 'banking' in merchant banking does not mean accepting deposits. A registered merchant banker cannot take deposits from the public; its business is fee-based advisory and issue management.
items.example: A company planning a ₹2,000 crore IPO appoints three BRLMs. One handles due diligence and the DRHP, another leads institutional marketing roadshows, the third coordinates retail distribution. They recommend a price band of ₹540–₹570 after studying peer valuations and investor feedback. After the issue, one BRLM acts as the coordinating lead manager and files post-issue reports with SEBI.
faqs: Is a merchant banker the same as a stock broker?

No. A stock broker executes buy and sell orders on exchanges for clients. A merchant banker manages capital raising and corporate actions for issuers. Some financial groups have both licences in different entities, but the roles, regulations and responsibilities are separate.
What is a due diligence certificate?

It is a certificate filed with SEBI by the lead merchant banker confirming that it has examined the issuer's documents and that the offer document gives true, fair and adequate disclosure for investors to make an informed decision. It creates legal accountability for the merchant banker.

items.title: Stock Broker Meaning: Role, Duties and Client Protections
items.description: What a SEBI-registered stock broker does, trading vs clearing members, the UCC, segregation of client funds, and protections investors should know about.
items.short: A stock broker is a SEBI-registered member of a stock exchange who places buy and sell orders on the exchange on behalf of clients and for its own account.
body: Only trading members of an exchange can enter orders into its trading system. Investors open trading accounts with brokers after KYC, sign the rights and obligations document and receive a unique client code (UCC) that identifies every order they place. Full-service brokers add research and advisory support; discount brokers focus on low-cost execution.

A trading member may also be a clearing member, settling its own trades, or may use a separate professional clearing member. Brokers must collect margins upfront from clients, report client-wise margin details to the clearing corporation, issue contract notes, maintain client funds separately from their own money and settle running accounts as per SEBI rules.

SEBI has strengthened client protection through several measures: upfront margin collection, direct payout of securities to client demat accounts, restrictions on using client funds, the DDPI framework replacing broad powers of attorney, and the requirement that associated persons pass the relevant NISM certification.

Investors should remember that a broker is an agent, not a guarantor of returns. If a broker defaults, the exchange's investor protection fund may compensate eligible claims within limits. Using a broker's 'tips' or letting the broker trade on your behalf without written authority are common sources of disputes.
items.example: Asha opens an account with a discount broker and gets UCC ABC1234. When she places an order to buy 10 shares, the broker tags the order with her UCC and sends it to the exchange. Her ₹15,000 margin is reported to the clearing corporation in her name. If the broker went bankrupt, the clearing corporation could identify her collateral by UCC, and her shares sit in her own demat account, not the broker's.
faqs: What is the difference between a trading member and a clearing member?

A trading member executes trades on the exchange. A clearing member clears and settles trades with the clearing corporation, including paying margins and settling funds and securities. Some brokers are both; others, called trading members only, settle through professional clearing members.
What is an authorised person (AP)?

An authorised person, earlier called a sub-broker in some contexts, is an agent appointed by a stock broker and approved by the exchange to bring in clients and provide access to the broker's trading platform. The broker remains responsible for the AP's activities towards clients.

items.title: What is a Derivative? Meaning, Types and Uses in India
items.description: Derivative meaning in finance explained simply: forwards, futures, options and swaps, the underlying asset, who uses derivatives and their main risks.
items.short: A derivative is a financial contract whose value is derived from the price of an underlying asset, such as a share, index, currency, commodity or interest rate.
body: The four basic types are forwards, futures, options and swaps. Forwards and swaps are mostly traded over the counter (OTC) between two parties, while futures and options in India are exchange-traded on NSE, BSE, MCX and NCDEX with a clearing corporation guaranteeing settlement. The Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act includes derivatives in the definition of securities, which brings exchange-traded derivatives under SEBI.

Derivatives have three main uses. Hedgers use them to reduce risk — an exporter locks in a rupee-dollar rate, a portfolio manager protects against a market fall. Speculators use them to take leveraged views on price movements. Arbitrageurs exploit price differences between related markets, such as the cash and futures markets, which keeps prices aligned.

Leverage is the defining feature: you control a large exposure by paying only a margin (for futures) or a premium (for options). This makes derivatives efficient for hedging and also dangerous for speculation. SEBI studies have found that most individual traders in equity F&O lose money, which led to measures in 2024 such as larger contract sizes and fewer weekly expiries.

A key misconception is that derivatives are separate from the 'real' market. Because arbitrage links them to the underlying, heavy derivatives activity can influence cash market prices, especially near expiry. Another is that derivatives are only for speculation; many of the largest users are banks, exporters and insurers managing risk.
items.example: A jeweller expects to buy 1 kg of gold in three months. Gold futures for that month trade at ₹72,000 per 10 grams. By buying futures equivalent to 1 kg, he fixes his cost at about ₹72 lakh. If gold rises to ₹76,000, his physical purchase costs ₹4 lakh more but his futures gain about ₹4 lakh; if gold falls to ₹69,000, the futures lose ₹3 lakh while his purchase is ₹3 lakh cheaper.
faqs: Are derivatives securities in India?

Yes. The Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 includes derivatives in the definition of securities, which is why exchange-traded equity, currency and commodity derivatives are regulated by SEBI. OTC derivatives involving banks, such as interest rate swaps and forex forwards, are regulated mainly by the RBI.
Why are derivatives considered risky?

Because of leverage. A small margin controls a large position, so a modest adverse move can wipe out the margin and create further losses. Options sellers can face very large losses, and option buyers often lose the entire premium. Understanding contract size, margins and risk is essential before trading.

items.title: Forward Contract Meaning: Example and Futures Difference
items.description: What a forward contract is, how Indian exporters use currency forwards, its counterparty and liquidity risks, and the key differences from futures.
items.short: A forward contract is a private agreement between two parties to buy or sell an asset at a fixed price on a specified future date.
body: Forwards are customised: the two parties decide the quantity, quality, price, delivery date and place. Nothing is paid upfront except, sometimes, collateral. On the settlement date, the asset is delivered against payment, or the difference is settled in cash. Because they are negotiated privately, forwards are over-the-counter (OTC) instruments.

In India, the most common forwards are currency forwards between banks and their customers. An exporter expecting dollars in three months can sell them forward to a bank at a rate fixed today. The forward rate reflects the spot rate adjusted for the interest rate difference between India and the US, called the forward premium.

The main drawbacks are counterparty risk — the other side may default — and lack of liquidity, since you cannot easily exit a customised contract before maturity. There is also limited price transparency. Futures were developed to address these issues by standardising contracts and placing a clearing corporation in the middle.

Exam questions often test the contrast: forwards are OTC, customised, settled at maturity and carry counterparty risk; futures are exchange-traded, standardised, marked to market daily and guaranteed by a clearing corporation. Remember that both create an obligation for both parties, unlike options.
items.example: An exporter will receive USD 1,00,000 in 90 days. Spot USD/INR is 84.00 and the bank quotes a 90-day forward rate of 84.45. The exporter sells USD forward at 84.45 and is assured ₹84,45,000. If the spot rate on the due date is 83.20, the exporter is protected — the open market would have given only ₹83,20,000. If it is 85.50, the exporter misses ₹1,05,000 of extra gain but has the certainty sought.
faqs: Can a forward contract be cancelled?

Yes, but only by agreement with the counterparty, usually at a cost. In bank currency forwards, early cancellation means the bank closes the deal at the current forward rate and the customer pays or receives the difference. There is no exchange where you can simply sell the contract to someone else.
Why are forward rates different from spot rates?

Forward rates reflect the interest rate difference between the two currencies. If Indian interest rates are higher than US rates, the dollar trades at a forward premium against the rupee. This is called interest rate parity and prevents risk-free profit from borrowing in one currency and investing in another.

items.title: Futures Contract Meaning: How Futures Trading Works
items.description: What a futures contract is, how it differs from a forward, lot size, margins, daily mark-to-market and expiry, with a worked Indian stock futures example.
items.short: A futures contract is a standardised, exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell an underlying asset at a set price on a future date, with daily settlement of gains and losses.
body: Futures standardise everything a forward leaves to negotiation: the underlying, the lot size, the expiry date and the settlement method. In India, futures trade on stocks, indices, currencies, interest rates and commodities. Equity futures expire on the scheduled expiry day of the month, and contracts for the near, next and far months trade simultaneously.

To take a position, both buyer and seller deposit an initial margin with their broker, calculated by the clearing corporation using SPAN plus exposure margin. Every day the position is marked to market: gains are credited and losses debited based on the daily settlement price. If losses reduce the margin below the required level, the trader must add funds.

Stock futures in India are physically settled at expiry, meaning open long positions must take delivery of shares and short positions must deliver them. Index futures are cash settled. Most traders close or roll over their positions before expiry rather than taking delivery.

The leverage is high: a 15–20% margin means a 5% price move can produce a 25–30% gain or loss on your capital. A common misunderstanding is that a futures buyer can lose only the margin. Losses are unlimited in theory; if the price keeps falling, the trader must keep paying mark-to-market losses.
items.example: A stock trades at ₹1,500 and its one-month futures at ₹1,510. Suppose the lot size is 500 shares, so one contract is worth ₹7,55,000, and the initial margin is about 20%, or ₹1,51,000. If the futures price rises to ₹1,560, the buyer gains ₹50 × 500 = ₹25,000 — about 16.6% of the margin. A fall to ₹1,460 causes an equal ₹25,000 loss, collected through daily mark-to-market.
faqs: What is rollover in futures?

Rollover means closing a position in the expiring contract and opening the same position in the next month's contract. It lets traders maintain exposure beyond expiry. The cost of rolling depends on the price difference between the two contracts, which reflects interest and expected dividends.
Do I need to pay the full value to buy futures?

No. You pay only the initial margin, a fraction of the contract value, and then settle daily gains or losses. This leverage is why futures need careful risk management: you are exposed to the full contract value even though you put up only part of it.

items.title: Options Contract Meaning: Rights, Premium and Types
items.description: What an options contract is, the rights of the buyer and obligations of the seller, calls and puts, strike price, premium and expiry, with simple examples.
items.short: An option is a contract that gives the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an underlying asset at a fixed price on or before a specified date.
body: Every option has a buyer (holder) and a seller (writer). The buyer pays a premium upfront for the right. The seller receives the premium and takes on the obligation to perform if the buyer exercises. A call option gives the right to buy; a put option gives the right to sell. The fixed price is the strike price, and the last date is the expiry.

This asymmetry is what makes options different from futures. The buyer's maximum loss is the premium paid, while the potential gain can be large. The seller's maximum gain is the premium received, while the potential loss can be large — unlimited for a naked call writer. Because of this, sellers must post margin, while buyers pay only the premium.

In India, exchange-traded equity options on indices and stocks are European style: they can be exercised only at expiry, though they can be sold anytime before. Index options are cash settled; in-the-money stock options are physically settled. Option prices are influenced by the underlying price, strike, time to expiry, volatility, interest rates and dividends.

Options are used for hedging (buying puts to protect a portfolio), income (writing covered calls), and speculation. A big misconception is that buying options is low risk because loss is limited. The loss is limited per trade, but the probability of losing the whole premium is high, especially for out-of-the-money options close to expiry.
items.example: A share trades at ₹1,000. Ravi buys a call with strike ₹1,050, paying a premium of ₹20 per share for a lot of 500 (₹10,000). At expiry: if the share is at ₹1,120, the call is worth ₹70, giving a profit of (₹70 − ₹20) × 500 = ₹25,000. If the share is at ₹1,040, the call expires worthless and Ravi loses ₹10,000. The seller's result is the exact opposite.
faqs: What is the difference between an option buyer and an option seller?

The buyer pays a premium and has a right but no obligation; maximum loss is the premium. The seller receives the premium and has an obligation if the buyer exercises; losses can be large. That is why exchanges collect margins from sellers but not from buyers.
Can I exit an option before expiry?

Yes. Although Indian equity options are European and can be exercised only at expiry, they trade on the exchange until expiry. You can square off by selling a bought option or buying back a sold one at the current premium, booking the profit or loss.

items.title: Call Option Meaning: Payoff, Breakeven and Example
items.description: Call option meaning explained with an Indian example: the right to buy at the strike price, buyer and seller payoffs, breakeven and when calls are used.
items.short: A call option gives its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy the underlying asset at the strike price on or before expiry, in exchange for a premium.
body: A call buyer benefits when the underlying price rises above the strike price. At expiry, the call's value is the greater of zero and (spot price − strike price). The buyer's profit is that value minus the premium paid, so the breakeven point is strike price plus premium. Below the strike, the call expires worthless and the buyer loses only the premium.

The call seller (writer) receives the premium and must deliver the underlying (or pay the difference in cash-settled contracts) if the option is exercised. The seller profits if the price stays below the breakeven, with maximum gain equal to the premium. If the price rises sharply, losses for a naked call writer have no upper limit.

Calls are used by traders expecting a rise, by investors who want upside with limited downside, and by those who hold shares and write calls to earn extra income (covered calls). Fund managers sometimes buy calls when they want market exposure but have cash yet to be deployed.

A common confusion: a call buyer does not need the price to just rise — it must rise enough to cover the premium before expiry. Time decay works against the buyer every day. Also, 'call' has nothing to do with phoning a broker or with callable bonds; it only means the right to call away (buy) the asset.
items.example: An index stands at 24,000. A trader buys a 24,200 call at a premium of 120 points, with an illustrative lot size of 75 (cost ₹9,000). Breakeven at expiry is 24,320. If the index settles at 24,500, the call is worth 300 points, giving a profit of (300 − 120) × 75 = ₹13,500. At 24,250 the call is worth 50, a loss of ₹5,250. Anywhere at or below 24,200, the full ₹9,000 is lost.
faqs: What is the maximum loss for a call option buyer?

The premium paid. If the underlying stays at or below the strike price at expiry, the call expires worthless and the buyer loses the entire premium, but nothing more. This defined risk is why many beginners buy calls, though the probability of losing the premium can be high.
What is the breakeven point of a call option?

For the buyer, the breakeven at expiry is strike price plus premium paid. Only above this level does the buyer make a net profit. For example, a ₹500 strike call bought at ₹15 breaks even at ₹515, ignoring brokerage and taxes.

items.title: Put Option Meaning: Payoff, Breakeven and Hedging Use
items.description: Put option meaning with a worked example: the right to sell at the strike price, buyer and seller payoffs, breakeven and how puts protect a portfolio.
items.short: A put option gives its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to sell the underlying asset at the strike price on or before expiry, in exchange for a premium.
body: A put buyer benefits when the underlying price falls below the strike price. At expiry, the put's value is the greater of zero and (strike price − spot price). Breakeven for the buyer is strike price minus premium. If the price stays above the strike, the put expires worthless and the buyer loses only the premium.

The put seller receives the premium and must buy the underlying at the strike (or pay the difference in cash) if exercised. The seller's maximum gain is the premium, while the maximum loss is large — up to the strike price minus the premium if the underlying falls to zero. Exchanges therefore require margins from put writers.

Puts are the classic insurance tool. An investor holding shares can buy puts to cap the downside; this is called a protective put. Traders expecting a fall can buy puts instead of short selling, with known maximum loss. Fund managers buy index puts to hedge portfolios during uncertain periods such as elections or budget announcements.

Beginners sometimes think buying a put means they must own the shares. You do not need to hold the underlying to buy a put; you profit from the fall in price. Another misunderstanding: a put writer is bullish or neutral, not bearish, since the writer wants the price to stay above the strike.
items.example: A share trades at ₹800. An investor buys a ₹780 put at ₹18 for a lot of 600 shares (premium ₹10,800). Breakeven is ₹762. If the share falls to ₹700 at expiry, the put is worth ₹80, a profit of (₹80 − ₹18) × 600 = ₹37,200. At ₹770 the put is worth ₹10, a net loss of ₹4,800. At ₹780 or above, the entire ₹10,800 is lost.
faqs: Is buying a put the same as short selling?

Both profit from falling prices, but the risk profiles differ. A short seller faces unlimited loss if prices rise, while a put buyer's loss is limited to the premium. Puts also have a fixed expiry, so the fall must happen within that time to be profitable.
Why would someone sell a put option?

Put writers collect premium and profit if the price stays above the strike. Some investors write puts on stocks they would be happy to buy at the strike price, effectively getting paid while waiting. The risk is a sharp fall, which forces them to buy at a price well above the market.

items.title: Option Premium Meaning: Intrinsic Value and Time Value
items.description: What an option premium is made of, how to calculate intrinsic value and time value for calls and puts, and the factors that push premiums up or down.
items.short: An option premium is the price paid by the buyer to the seller, made up of intrinsic value (what the option is worth if exercised now) and time value.
body: Intrinsic value is the amount by which an option is in the money. For a call, it is the greater of zero and (spot − strike); for a put, the greater of zero and (strike − spot). It can never be negative. At-the-money and out-of-the-money options have zero intrinsic value, so their entire premium is time value.

Time value equals premium minus intrinsic value. It reflects the chance that the option becomes more valuable before expiry. It is highest for at-the-money options and falls as expiry approaches — a process called time decay (measured by theta). At expiry, time value is zero and the premium equals intrinsic value.

Six factors drive premiums: price of the underlying, strike price, time to expiry, volatility, interest rates and expected dividends. Higher volatility increases both call and put premiums because a larger move becomes more likely. More time to expiry generally increases premiums. Rising interest rates slightly increase call premiums and reduce put premiums, while dividends do the reverse.

Many traders think a cheap option is a bargain. A low premium usually means the option is far out of the money with a small chance of paying off. Comparing premiums across strikes without looking at intrinsic and time value leads to poor decisions.
items.example: Spot ₹2,150. A ₹2,100 call trades at ₹78: intrinsic value ₹50 (2,150 − 2,100), time value ₹28. A ₹2,200 call trades at ₹30: intrinsic value zero, time value ₹30. A ₹2,200 put trades at ₹76: intrinsic value ₹50 (2,200 − 2,150), time value ₹26. If nothing else changes, by expiry the ₹2,100 call will be worth only ₹50 and the ₹2,200 call nothing.
faqs: Can an option trade below its intrinsic value?

For European options, slight deviations can occur, especially in illiquid strikes or for deep in-the-money puts when interest rates are high. In liquid markets, large gaps are quickly removed by arbitrage. For practical purposes, assume premium is at least close to intrinsic value.
Why do premiums rise before events like results or the Budget?

Uncertainty raises expected volatility. Traders anticipate larger price moves, so implied volatility rises and both call and put premiums increase. After the event, implied volatility often drops sharply, a fall sometimes called a volatility crush, which can hurt option buyers even if the price moves.

items.title: ITM, ATM, OTM Options Meaning: In, At and Out of the Money
items.description: In-the-money, at-the-money and out-of-the-money options explained for calls and puts, with a strike table, intrinsic value and why moneyness matters.
items.short: Moneyness describes an option's strike price relative to the current underlying price: in the money (ITM), at the money (ATM) or out of the money (OTM).
body: For a call, the option is ITM when the spot price is above the strike, ATM when spot is at (or nearest to) the strike, and OTM when spot is below the strike. For a put, it is the reverse: ITM when spot is below the strike, OTM when spot is above. Only ITM options have intrinsic value.

Moneyness changes the option's behaviour. Deep ITM options behave almost like the underlying — their delta is close to 1 (or −1 for puts) and their premium is mostly intrinsic value. ATM options have the highest time value and the most sensitivity to time decay and volatility. Deep OTM options are cheap, with low delta and a low chance of paying off.

On expiry day, moneyness decides settlement. ITM index options are cash settled for their intrinsic value. ITM stock options lead to physical delivery of shares. Exchanges also have rules about close-to-money stock options, so traders should check exchange rules on expiry-day risk.

A frequent exam trap is applying call logic to puts. A put with strike ₹500 when the spot is ₹520 is OTM, not ITM. Another is assuming the ATM strike must match spot exactly — in practice, the ATM strike is the one closest to the spot price.
items.example: Spot ₹1,020, strikes in steps of ₹20. Calls: ₹980 and ₹1,000 are ITM (intrinsic ₹40 and ₹20), ₹1,020 is ATM, ₹1,040 and ₹1,060 are OTM. Puts: ₹1,040 and ₹1,060 are ITM (intrinsic ₹20 and ₹40), ₹1,020 is ATM, ₹980 and ₹1,000 are OTM. If spot moves to ₹1,050, the ₹1,040 call becomes ITM and the ₹1,040 put becomes OTM.
faqs: Which is better to buy: ITM, ATM or OTM options?

There is no universally better choice; it is a trade-off. ITM options cost more but move more like the underlying and lose less to time decay proportionally. OTM options are cheaper but need a bigger move to profit. ATM options are most sensitive to volatility and time. The choice depends on the view and risk appetite.
Is an ATM option in the money at expiry?

Only if the spot moves past the strike in the favourable direction. Exactly at the strike, intrinsic value is zero for both the call and the put. In practice, the settlement price usually differs slightly from the strike, making one side marginally ITM.

items.title: European vs American Options: Exercise Style Difference
items.description: Difference between European and American options, why Indian equity options are European, how exercise style affects pricing and early exercise decisions.
items.short: A European option can be exercised only on its expiry date, while an American option can be exercised on any day up to and including expiry.
body: The names have nothing to do with geography; both types trade worldwide. The difference is purely about when the holder can exercise. Because an American option gives the holder an extra right — early exercise — its premium is at least equal to, and sometimes more than, an otherwise identical European option.

In India, all exchange-traded equity options, both index and stock, are European. Stock options were American style when introduced in 2001 but were converted to European style around 2011. Currency options on Indian exchanges are also European. Commodity options on MCX have their own exercise rules set by the exchange.

European exercise does not mean you are locked in. You can always sell the option in the market before expiry. In fact, for American calls on non-dividend-paying stocks, early exercise is rarely optimal because selling captures the remaining time value, while exercising throws it away.

Pricing models differ too. The Black-Scholes model was built for European options. American options need methods such as binomial trees that allow for early exercise. Exam questions often ask which style Indian options follow, and whether a European option can be traded before expiry (yes).
items.example: A trader holds a European call with strike ₹500 on a share now at ₹560, with 10 days to expiry; the option trades at ₹64. Exercise is not allowed before expiry, but selling it in the market gives ₹64 per share. Even if the call were American, exercising now would give only ₹60 of intrinsic value, losing ₹4 of time value — so selling is better in either case.
faqs: Are Indian stock options American or European?

European. Indian stock options and index options on NSE and BSE can be exercised only on the expiry day. In-the-money stock options are physically settled at expiry, and index options are cash settled. Positions can be closed at any time before expiry by trading on the exchange.
When does early exercise of an American option make sense?

Early exercise of a call may make sense just before a large dividend, when the dividend exceeds the remaining time value. Deep in-the-money American puts may also be exercised early when interest rates are high. Otherwise, selling the option usually captures more value than exercising it.

items.title: Open Interest Meaning in F&O: How to Read OI Data
items.description: Open interest explained: how OI is counted in futures and options, how it differs from volume, and what rising or falling OI with price changes may signal.
items.short: Open interest is the total number of outstanding derivative contracts that have been opened and not yet closed, exercised or expired at a given time.
body: Each contract has a buyer and a seller, but open interest counts it only once. OI rises when a new buyer and a new seller create a fresh position. It falls when an existing buyer and existing seller both close positions. If one side closes and the other is newly opened (an existing position transferred to a new trader), OI stays unchanged.

Volume and OI measure different things. Volume counts all contracts traded during the day, including intraday trades that are opened and closed. OI is a snapshot of positions still open at the end of the day (or at a point in time). A contract can have high volume and low OI if most trading is intraday.

Traders combine price and OI changes for clues. Price up with OI up is read as long build-up; price down with OI up as short build-up; price up with OI down as short covering; price down with OI down as long unwinding. In options, strikes with very large call OI or put OI are sometimes viewed as resistance or support levels.

These are interpretations, not rules. Large OI can come from hedgers and arbitrageurs, not just directional traders. Exchanges also set market-wide position limits in terms of OI, and stocks crossing 95% of their limit enter a ban period in which new F&O positions are not allowed.
items.example: On Monday, A buys 1 futures contract from B: OI = 1. On Tuesday, C buys 2 contracts from D (both new): OI = 3. On Wednesday, A sells his 1 contract to E, a new trader: OI stays 3 — the position simply changed hands. On Thursday, C sells 2 contracts to D, closing both positions: OI falls to 1. Total volume over four days was 6 contracts.
faqs: What is the difference between volume and open interest?

Volume counts every contract traded in a period, while open interest counts the contracts still open at a point in time. If a trader buys and sells the same contract in a day, volume rises by two transactions while open interest does not change. OI shows positions carried; volume shows activity.
Does high open interest mean the price will go up?

No. High open interest only means many positions are open. Whether those positions are long or short, hedges or speculative bets, cannot be determined from OI alone. Traders look at the combination of price movement and change in OI, but these signals are probabilistic, not certain.

items.title: Mark-to-Market (MTM) Meaning in Futures with Example
items.description: What mark-to-market means in futures trading: daily settlement price, how profits and losses are credited or debited each day and why it limits default risk.
items.short: Mark-to-market is the daily revaluation of open futures positions at the settlement price, with gains credited and losses debited to traders' accounts every day.
body: In a forward contract, gains and losses build up until maturity, which increases the chance that the losing side cannot pay. Futures avoid this by settling the change in value every trading day. The clearing corporation calculates a daily settlement price, usually based on the closing price, and each open position is revalued against it.

On the first day, MTM is calculated as (settlement price − trade price) × quantity for a long position. On later days, it is (today's settlement price − yesterday's settlement price) × quantity. Losses must be paid in cash by the next morning, and profits are released to the trader. After each day's settlement, the position effectively carries the new settlement price.

MTM losses are separate from the initial margin. If losses shrink the account below the maintenance level, the broker asks for more funds (a margin call). If the client does not pay, the broker can close the position. This daily discipline keeps the clearing corporation's exposure to a single day's price change, backed by margins.

The term also appears in accounting and in bond valuations, where 'marking to market' means valuing assets at current market prices instead of cost. In derivatives exams, focus on the daily cash flow mechanism and remember that options buyers do not face daily MTM on their long positions — they pay the premium upfront.
items.example: Priya buys 1 lot of 400 shares in stock futures at ₹950 on Monday. Settlement prices: Monday ₹958, Tuesday ₹944, Wednesday ₹961. Her MTM: Monday (958 − 950) × 400 = +₹3,200; Tuesday (944 − 958) × 400 = −₹5,600; Wednesday (961 − 944) × 400 = +₹6,800. Net so far +₹4,400, which equals (961 − 950) × 400 — the daily flows add up to her total gain.
faqs: Is MTM loss a real loss if I haven't closed my position?

Yes, in cash terms. MTM losses are actually debited from your account daily, even if you keep the position open. If the price later recovers, you get MTM credits back. The final profit or loss equals the sum of all daily MTM flows plus the closing difference.
Do options have mark-to-market settlement?

Option buyers pay the full premium upfront, so their positions are not subject to daily MTM cash settlement. Option sellers' positions are revalued daily for margin purposes, and margin requirements can rise sharply if the market moves against them, but premium is settled upfront rather than through daily MTM.

items.title: SPAN Margin Meaning: Initial and Exposure Margin in F&O
items.description: How SPAN margin works for futures and options in India, the role of exposure margin, portfolio-based margining and why margin requirements change daily.
items.short: SPAN margin is the initial margin for derivatives positions, computed by a risk model that estimates the worst likely one-day loss on a portfolio.
body: SPAN stands for Standard Portfolio Analysis of Risk, a system developed by the Chicago Mercantile Exchange and used by Indian clearing corporations. It simulates a set of scenarios — combinations of price moves and volatility changes — for each position and works out the largest likely loss across the portfolio. That figure becomes the SPAN, or initial, margin.

Because SPAN looks at the whole portfolio, offsetting positions get credit. A long futures position combined with a long put on the same underlying needs less margin than the futures alone, since the put limits the downside. This is why hedged option strategies often need far less margin than naked option selling.

On top of SPAN, the clearing corporation collects an exposure margin (also called extreme loss margin, ELM) as a cushion for moves beyond the SPAN scenarios. SEBI has added further requirements over time, such as extra margins on short options on expiry day and upfront collection of the full margin, under the peak margin framework. Specific percentages are revised often — check the clearing corporation's latest circulars.

A frequent misconception is that margin is a fee. It is collateral, returned when the position is closed, adjusted for profits and losses. Another is that margin requirements stay fixed; they change daily with volatility, and can jump during market stress, forcing traders to add funds or cut positions.
items.example: A trader sells 1 lot of index futures worth ₹18,00,000. SPAN margin is, say, ₹1,80,000 and exposure margin ₹36,000, a total of ₹2,16,000. If she also buys an out-of-the-money call that caps her loss on a sharp rise, SPAN recalculates the worst-case loss for the combined position, and the requirement might fall to around ₹1,10,000 in this illustration. Actual amounts come from the exchange's margin calculator.
faqs: What is the difference between SPAN margin and exposure margin?

SPAN margin covers the likely worst one-day loss estimated through risk scenarios. Exposure margin is an additional buffer for extreme moves not captured by SPAN, set as a percentage of contract value. Together they form the initial margin a trader must have before taking a futures or short options position.
Why is margin lower for hedged positions?

SPAN evaluates risk at the portfolio level. When positions offset each other, the worst-case loss is smaller than the sum of individual worst cases, so the required margin falls. This encourages hedging and explains why spreads often need much less margin than single naked option sales.

items.title: Cost of Carry and Basis in Futures: Formula and Example
items.description: How futures prices relate to spot prices through cost of carry, the formula with interest and dividends, what basis means and why it converges at expiry.
items.short: Cost of carry is the net cost of holding an asset until a futures contract's expiry; basis is the difference between the futures price and the spot price.
body: The cost-of-carry model says a fair futures price equals the spot price plus the cost of financing it until expiry, minus any income the asset generates. For a stock or index, the main cost is interest and the main income is dividends: F = S × (1 + r × t) − D, in simple-interest form, where r is the annual rate and t the fraction of a year. For commodities, storage and insurance costs are added.

Basis is commonly defined in equity derivatives texts as futures price minus spot price; some commodity texts use spot minus futures. Whichever convention is used, basis is not constant: it shrinks as expiry nears because the financing period gets shorter. On expiry, the futures price converges to the spot price and basis becomes zero.

If futures trade well above the fair value, arbitrageurs buy in the cash market and sell futures (cash-and-carry arbitrage). If futures trade below fair value, they do the reverse. This activity keeps futures close to the cost-of-carry price in liquid contracts.

Many traders assume futures above spot means the market expects a rise. Usually it simply reflects interest cost. Conversely, a futures price below spot can occur when a large dividend is due before expiry, not necessarily because of bearish sentiment.
items.example: A stock is at ₹2,000 and the risk-free rate is 7% a year. For a 30-day future with no dividend, fair price ≈ 2,000 × (1 + 0.07 × 30/365) = ₹2,011.51, so basis is about ₹11.51. If a ₹15 dividend is due before expiry, fair price ≈ ₹1,996.51 — below spot. With 5 days left (no dividend), fair price ≈ ₹2,001.92; on expiry, futures equals spot.
faqs: Why do futures usually trade above spot?

Because buying the asset today requires money that could otherwise earn interest. A futures buyer avoids this financing cost, so the futures price includes it. When the interest cost exceeds income from the asset, such as dividends, futures trade above spot. This is called a positive cost of carry.
What is convergence in futures?

Convergence means the futures price moves towards the spot price as expiry approaches, because the cost of carry shrinks with time. On the final settlement day, the futures price equals the spot price. Arbitrageurs rely on convergence to lock in profits when the basis is mispriced.

items.title: Contango vs Backwardation Meaning in Futures Markets
items.description: Contango and backwardation explained with Indian commodity and equity examples: why far-month futures can trade above or below near-month and spot prices.
items.short: Contango is when futures prices are above the spot price (and later expiries higher still); backwardation is when futures trade below the spot price.
body: In a normal market for financial assets and storable commodities, futures trade at a premium to spot because of interest and storage costs. This upward-sloping structure — near month above spot, next month higher, far month highest — is called contango. Most Indian index futures and gold futures are in contango most of the time.

Backwardation occurs when futures prices are below spot. It happens when holding the physical asset gives a benefit, called the convenience yield — for example, a shortage of a commodity in the current season, or when a big dividend is expected before expiry in an equity future. Agricultural commodities often show backwardation just before a new harvest arrives, since prices are expected to fall.

The structure matters for rolling positions. A long futures holder in contango pays more for each new contract when rolling over, which eats into returns over time. In backwardation, rolling a long position earns a gain. Commodity ETFs and long-term hedgers watch this closely.

Students often confuse contango with a bullish view and backwardation with a bearish view. The curve mainly reflects carrying costs, supply conditions and convenience yield, not simply market sentiment.
items.example: Gold spot ₹72,000 per 10 g. MCX futures: 2-month ₹72,950, 4-month ₹73,900 — contango, since each later month is higher (roughly ₹475 per month reflecting carrying costs). A pulse futures market just before harvest shows spot ₹7,800 per quintal, near month ₹7,650 and next month ₹7,400 — backwardation, because the market expects a large new crop to push prices down.
faqs: Is contango good or bad for investors?

It depends on the position. Long futures holders who roll repeatedly lose some return in contango because each new contract costs more. Short futures holders gain from the roll. For someone simply hedging a single future purchase, contango is just the cost of locking in a price.
What is convenience yield?

Convenience yield is the benefit of holding the physical commodity rather than a futures contract, such as being able to keep a factory running during a shortage. When this benefit is high, spot prices can rise above futures prices, producing backwardation.

items.title: Hedging Meaning in Derivatives: Hedge Ratio and Examples
items.description: What hedging means, how investors and businesses hedge with futures and options in India, the beta-based hedge ratio formula and the limits of hedging.
items.short: Hedging is taking a position in a derivative that offsets the risk of an existing or expected position in the underlying asset, reducing the impact of adverse price moves.
body: Hedgers want protection, not profit. An investor holding shares can sell index futures or buy puts; an importer can buy dollar futures; a farmer can sell agricultural futures before harvest. If the price moves against the physical position, the derivative gains, and vice versa. The result is a more predictable outcome.

The hedge ratio decides how much derivative to use. For a stock portfolio hedged with index futures, a common approach uses beta: number of contracts = (portfolio value × portfolio beta) ÷ (futures price × lot size). A portfolio with beta 1.2 needs 20% more index futures than its rupee value to offset market movements.

Hedging has costs and limitations. Futures hedges remove upside as well as downside. Options hedges keep the upside but cost premium. Basis risk remains when the hedge instrument does not move exactly like the asset — for example, hedging a mid-cap portfolio with Nifty futures. Hedges also need to be rolled at expiry.

A misconception is that a hedged position cannot lose money. It can, through basis risk, imperfect ratios, timing mismatches and costs. Another is that a successful hedge is one that makes profit. A good hedge reduces variability; if the derivative leg loses money because the main position gained, the hedge did its job.
items.example: A fund holds a ₹5 crore portfolio with a beta of 1.2. Index futures trade at 24,500 with an illustrative lot size of 75, so one contract is worth ₹18,37,500. Contracts needed = (₹5,00,00,000 × 1.2) ÷ ₹18,37,500 ≈ 32.7, so it sells about 33 lots. If the index falls 5%, the portfolio is expected to lose about 6% (₹30 lakh), while the short futures gain about ₹30.3 lakh.
faqs: What is basis risk in hedging?

Basis risk is the risk that the hedge instrument and the asset being hedged do not move exactly together. For example, an investor hedging a pharma portfolio with Nifty futures is exposed if pharma stocks fall while the Nifty rises. Basis risk also arises when the hedge expires before or after the underlying exposure.
Is buying a put better than selling futures for hedging?

Each has trade-offs. Selling futures has no upfront cost but gives up gains if prices rise. Buying puts costs premium but keeps upside potential while limiting downside. The choice depends on cost tolerance, outlook and whether the hedger wants to keep participating in gains.

items.title: Arbitrage Meaning: Cash-Futures Arbitrage with Example
items.description: What arbitrage is in financial markets, how cash-and-carry and reverse arbitrage work between Indian cash and futures markets, and the costs that limit it.
items.short: Arbitrage is the practice of simultaneously buying and selling the same or equivalent assets in different markets to lock in a low-risk profit from a price difference.
body: In theory, arbitrage requires no capital and no risk; in practice, it needs capital, costs money to execute and carries small risks. The most common form in India is cash-futures arbitrage.
