If a stock's futures price is higher than the spot price plus cost of carry, an arbitrageur buys the shares and sells the futures, earning the difference at expiry when prices converge. This is called cash-and-carry arbitrage.

Reverse cash-and-carry is the opposite: when futures trade below fair value, arbitrageurs sell shares they hold (or borrow) and buy futures. Other forms include inter-exchange arbitrage (price differences between NSE and BSE), calendar spreads between months and options-based arbitrage using put-call parity.

Arbitrage keeps prices efficient. Because many players watch for mispricing, gaps close quickly. Arbitrage mutual funds in India use cash-futures strategies, earning returns broadly linked to short-term interest rates, with low equity market risk.

Costs and frictions are crucial: brokerage, STT, stamp duty, impact cost, margin funding and the risk that an arbitrage position must be unwound early. A price gap that looks profitable on paper may disappear after costs. Exam questions often ask what arbitrageurs do when futures are overpriced (buy spot, sell futures).
items.example: A stock trades at ₹1,000 in the cash market and its one-month futures at ₹1,015. Fair value at 7% for 30 days is about ₹1,005.75. An arbitrageur buys 1,000 shares for ₹10,00,000 and sells one lot of 1,000 futures at ₹1,015. At expiry, both settle at the same price, so the gross profit is ₹15,000 — about 1.5% for the month, or roughly 18% annualised, before costs, which then attract more arbitrageurs until the gap narrows.
faqs: Is arbitrage completely risk-free?

Not in practice. Execution risk (one leg filling at a worse price), changes in margin requirements, dividend surprises, early unwinding and transaction costs can reduce or eliminate profit. These risks are small compared with directional trading, which is why arbitrage returns are usually close to short-term interest rates.
Who are arbitrageurs in Indian markets?

Proprietary trading desks of brokers, banks, arbitrage mutual funds, some hedge-fund-style AIFs and high-frequency traders. Their activity keeps futures prices close to fair value and links the cash and derivatives markets. Individual traders rarely compete effectively because of costs and speed.

items.title: Lot Size in F&O: Meaning, Contract Value and SEBI Rules
items.description: What lot size means in futures and options, how contract value is calculated, SEBI's minimum contract value rules and how lot sizes change after revisions.
items.short: Lot size is the fixed number of units of the underlying in one futures or options contract, set by the exchange; it determines the contract's rupee value.
body: Exchange-traded derivatives are standardised, so you cannot buy 37 shares' worth of a stock future — you trade in multiples of the lot size. Contract value equals lot size × futures price (or, for options, lot size × strike or underlying price for exposure purposes; the premium paid is lot size × option price).

SEBI sets a minimum contract value for equity derivatives, and exchanges fix lot sizes to meet it. In late 2024, SEBI raised the minimum contract value for index derivatives to a range of about ₹15–20 lakh at the time of review, mainly to reduce participation by small, high-risk retail traders. Lot sizes are reviewed periodically and adjusted as prices move — always check the exchange's current lot size file.

Lot sizes also change after corporate actions. A stock split or bonus increases the lot size proportionately while adjusting the strike prices and futures prices, so the value of open positions does not change.

Beginners often look only at the option premium per unit, say ₹40, and underestimate the actual cash needed. With a lot of 75, that is ₹3,000; with a lot of 1,200, it is ₹48,000. Likewise, a ₹10 move in a futures price means very different profits or losses depending on lot size.
items.example: A stock future trades at ₹620 with a lot size of 1,250, so contract value is ₹7,75,000. If the price rises to ₹1,250 over a year, the exchange's next review may reduce the lot size so the contract value stays in range — for instance, to 600, giving ₹7,50,000. A call option at a premium of ₹14.50 on the original lot costs ₹18,125.
faqs: Can I trade less than one lot in futures and options?

No. Exchange-traded derivatives can be traded only in whole lots. If you want smaller exposure, you have to use the cash market or products such as ETFs. This standardisation is what makes exchange-traded contracts liquid and easy to clear.
Why did SEBI increase the contract size for index derivatives?

SEBI found that most individual traders in equity F&O were losing money. Raising the minimum contract value, along with measures like reducing weekly expiries, was meant to ensure that participants have adequate capital and risk capacity. Check SEBI's circulars for the current thresholds.

items.title: Physical Settlement in F&O: Stock Futures and Options Expiry
items.description: How physical settlement of stock futures and options works at expiry in India, delivery obligations for ITM options and margins in the days before expiry.
items.short: Physical settlement means that at expiry, open stock futures and in-the-money stock options are settled by actual delivery of shares rather than by a cash difference.
body: SEBI moved stock derivatives in India from cash settlement to compulsory physical settlement in phases between 2018 and 2019. Index derivatives remain cash settled because an index cannot be delivered. Physical settlement aligns the derivatives market more closely with the cash market and reduces manipulation through settlement prices.

At expiry, a long stock futures position must take delivery and pay the full value of the shares; a short position must deliver the shares. For options, an in-the-money long call leads to buying shares at the strike, a short call leads to delivering shares, a long put leads to delivering shares and a short put leads to receiving shares and paying the strike.

Because delivery needs full money or shares, brokers and clearing corporations levy increasing delivery margins in the days before expiry for positions likely to be settled physically. Many brokers square off open positions themselves before expiry if clients lack funds or shares. The settlement follows the normal equity cash market cycle.

Traders are sometimes caught off guard by a cheap option that ends slightly in the money at expiry, creating a large delivery obligation. Others forget that a short put that expires ITM means they must pay for the full lot of shares. Checking expiry-day exposure is essential.
items.example: Arun holds 1 lot (700 shares) of a ₹900 call on a stock that settles at ₹912 on expiry. The call is ITM, so he must buy 700 shares at ₹900 — paying ₹6,30,000 — and receives shares worth ₹6,38,400. If he has only ₹50,000 in his account, his broker will likely square off the call before expiry. The writer of that call must deliver 700 shares or face short-delivery consequences.
faqs: Are index options physically settled?

No. Index futures and options are cash settled because an index is not a deliverable asset. Only stock futures and in-the-money stock options are physically settled at expiry. Currency and some commodity derivatives have their own settlement rules set by the exchanges.
How can I avoid physical delivery in stock F&O?

Close or roll over positions before expiry. Most brokers also have their own cut-off times after which they square off open positions that could lead to delivery. If you intend to take or give delivery, ensure you have the full funds or shares ready in advance.

items.title: MWPL and F&O Ban Period: Position Limits Explained
items.description: What market-wide position limits and client position limits are, why stocks enter the F&O ban period at 95% of MWPL and what traders can and cannot do.
items.short: Position limits cap how many derivative contracts a client, broker or the whole market can hold in an underlying; MWPL is the market-wide limit for a stock's derivatives.
body: Position limits prevent any single participant from controlling an outsized share of a contract and reduce the risk of manipulation and settlement stress. Exchanges set limits at three levels: the market as a whole (market-wide position limit, MWPL), trading or clearing members, and individual clients. Index derivatives have separate limits based on gross open positions.

For individual stocks, the MWPL is based on the stock's free float and trading activity. When aggregate open interest across all participants exceeds 95% of the MWPL, the stock enters a ban period. During the ban, traders can only reduce existing positions; any increase attracts penalties. The ban lifts when open interest falls below a lower threshold, traditionally 80% of MWPL.

SEBI revised the methodology in 2025, including the way open interest is measured for options (moving towards delta-based or future-equivalent measures) and the way MWPL is computed. Exact formulas and thresholds should be checked in the latest SEBI and exchange circulars.

Traders sometimes believe a ban means no trading in the stock at all. The cash market continues normally, and existing F&O positions can be closed. The ban only stops fresh positions that would increase open interest.
items.example: A stock's MWPL is 20 crore shares. Its open interest across futures and options reaches 19.1 crore — 95.5% of MWPL — so it enters the ban from the next trading day. A trader who is short 3 lots may buy them back, but cannot add a fourth. Over a few sessions, positions are unwound and OI drops to 15.8 crore (79%), so the stock exits the ban.
faqs: What happens if I increase my position during an F&O ban?

Exchanges levy a penalty on clients and brokers who increase open positions in a banned stock, and brokers usually block such orders. The penalty is calculated on the increase in position value. Closing or reducing existing positions is permitted throughout the ban period.
Do position limits apply to index derivatives?

Yes, but differently. Index derivatives are not subject to stock-style ban periods. Instead, exchanges set position limits for trading members, foreign portfolio investors, mutual funds and clients, often linked to total open interest or fixed rupee amounts. SEBI also introduced intraday monitoring of index derivatives positions.

items.title: Index Futures Meaning: Nifty and Bank Nifty Futures
items.description: What index futures are, how Nifty and other index futures are priced, settled in cash and used for hedging portfolios, with a worked profit and loss example.
items.short: Index futures are futures contracts whose underlying is a stock market index such as the Nifty 50 or Sensex, settled in cash at expiry.
body: Index futures let investors take a view on the whole market, or hedge a portfolio, with a single contract. In India they trade on NSE (Nifty 50, Nifty Bank and others) and BSE (Sensex, Bankex). Contracts for the near, next and far months trade simultaneously, and each has a lot size fixed by the exchange to meet SEBI's minimum contract value.

Because an index cannot be delivered, settlement is in cash. Daily mark-to-market uses the futures closing price, and final settlement uses the closing value of the index on expiry day. Since 2025, SEBI has allowed each exchange to choose either Tuesday or Thursday as its expiry day for equity derivatives, so check the exchange calendar for current expiry dates.

Index futures are priced using the cost-of-carry model: spot index plus interest minus expected dividends from the constituent stocks. They are useful for hedging diversified portfolios — a fund manager expecting short-term volatility can sell index futures instead of selling dozens of stocks, avoiding transaction costs and taxes on the portfolio.

Index futures carry less single-stock risk than stock futures, but they are still leveraged. A move of a few hundred points can produce gains or losses equal to the full margin. Another misconception is that index futures are physically settled in the constituent shares; they are not.
items.example: The Nifty is at 24,000 and the one-month future at 24,140. With an illustrative lot size of 75, contract value is ₹18,10,500. A trader buys 1 lot. If the index future rises to 24,600 when he exits, the gain is 460 × 75 = ₹34,500. If it falls to 23,800, the loss is 340 × 75 = ₹25,500 — collected through daily MTM along the way.
faqs: Why are index futures cash settled?

An index is a calculated number representing a basket of stocks. Delivering every constituent in the right proportions would be impractical, so contracts are settled by paying the difference between the contract price and the final settlement index value. Cash settlement keeps index derivatives simple and liquid.
Can index futures hedge any portfolio?

They work best for diversified portfolios that move broadly with the index. Portfolios concentrated in mid-caps, small-caps or a single sector face basis risk, because their returns may diverge from the index. Using beta to size the hedge helps, but does not remove this mismatch fully.

items.title: Option Delta Meaning: Range, Calculation and Example
items.description: What option delta measures, its range for calls and puts, delta of ITM, ATM and OTM options, and how traders use it for hedging and delta-neutral trades.
items.short: Delta measures how much an option's premium is expected to change for a ₹1 change in the price of the underlying asset.
body: Call deltas range from 0 to 1, and put deltas from −1 to 0. A call with delta 0.6 should gain about ₹0.60 when the underlying rises by ₹1; a put with delta −0.4 should gain about ₹0.40 when the underlying falls by ₹1. At-the-money options have deltas near ±0.5, deep in-the-money options near ±1, and far out-of-the-money options near 0.

Delta also gives the equivalent position in the underlying. One lot of calls with delta 0.6 behaves like 60% of a lot of the underlying for small moves. Option writers use delta to hedge: a short call with delta 0.6 on 500 shares can be offset by buying 300 shares, making the position delta-neutral for small moves.

Delta is not fixed. It changes as the underlying price moves (measured by gamma), as time passes and as volatility changes. Near expiry, ATM option deltas swing quickly between 0 and 1, which makes hedging difficult. Many traders also use delta as a rough probability that the option will expire in the money, though this is only an approximation.

A common slip is to forget the sign. Long calls and short puts have positive delta (they gain when price rises); long puts and short calls have negative delta. Adding deltas across positions gives the portfolio's net directional exposure.
items.example: A stock trades at ₹800 and a ₹780 call has delta 0.62; the lot size is 500. If the stock rises to ₹810, the call premium should rise by about 0.62 × ₹10 = ₹6.20, or ₹3,100 per lot. A trader who sold 2 lots of this call has a delta of −0.62 × 1,000 = −620 shares; buying 620 shares would make the position approximately delta-neutral.
faqs: What is the delta of an at-the-money option?

Roughly 0.5 for a call and −0.5 for a put. In practice, because of interest rates and the way the Black-Scholes formula works, ATM call deltas are often a little above 0.5. As expiry approaches, the ATM delta becomes more sensitive and can jump quickly towards 0 or 1.
What does delta-neutral mean?

A delta-neutral position has a total delta of about zero, so small moves in the underlying do not change its value much. Option market makers and volatility traders use it to remove directional risk and focus on volatility or time decay. The position must be rebalanced as delta changes.

items.title: Option Gamma Meaning: How Delta Changes with Price
items.description: Gamma explained simply: how fast an option's delta changes, why gamma peaks for at-the-money options near expiry and why short-gamma positions are risky.
items.short: Gamma measures how much an option's delta changes for a ₹1 change in the price of the underlying asset.
body: If delta is the speed at which an option's price changes, gamma is the acceleration. Both calls and puts have positive gamma for the buyer and negative gamma for the seller. A gamma of 0.004 means delta rises by 0.004 for every ₹1 rise in the underlying (and falls by the same for a ₹1 drop).

Gamma is highest for at-the-money options and lowest for deep in-the-money or far out-of-the-money options. It also rises sharply as expiry approaches for ATM options, because a small move can decide whether the option ends with value or worthless. This is why expiry-day option prices swing so wildly.

Long-gamma positions (bought options) benefit from big moves in either direction: delta grows in the favourable direction as the price moves. Short-gamma positions (sold options) suffer from big moves: the position becomes increasingly exposed in the wrong direction. Option sellers who hedge with delta must keep buying high and selling low as gamma pushes their delta around.

Students often think gamma only matters to professionals. In practice, it explains why a short straddle that looks safe in the morning can lose heavily by afternoon on expiry day. High gamma combined with leverage is the main reason expiry-day option selling is risky.
items.example: A call has delta 0.50 and gamma 0.004 per ₹1. If the stock rises ₹20, delta becomes about 0.50 + 0.004 × 20 = 0.58. The premium rises not by 0.50 × 20 = ₹10 but by roughly the average delta × 20 = 0.54 × 20 = ₹10.80. On a lot of 1,000, that is ₹10,800 instead of ₹10,000 — the extra ₹800 is the gamma effect, which favours the buyer and hurts the seller.
faqs: Is high gamma good or bad?

It depends on whether you are long or short options. Buyers have positive gamma, so large moves help them. Sellers have negative gamma, so large moves hurt them progressively. High gamma generally comes with high theta, so buyers pay for gamma through faster time decay.
Why does gamma increase near expiry?

With little time left, an at-the-money option's delta can swing from near 0 to near 1 with a small move, because the outcome of finishing in or out of the money becomes very sensitive to price. That rapid change in delta is high gamma.

items.title: Option Theta Meaning: Time Decay Explained with Example
items.description: What theta means for option buyers and sellers, how time decay accelerates near expiry, why ATM options lose the most and how theta interacts with gamma.
items.short: Theta measures how much an option's premium is expected to fall with the passage of one day, assuming other factors stay the same.
body: Options lose time value as expiry approaches because there is less time for a favourable move. Theta is usually expressed as a negative number per day for a long option: a theta of −0.48 means the option loses about ₹0.48 per unit each day. For the seller, the same theta is a daily gain.

Time decay is not linear. It is slow when expiry is months away and accelerates in the last few weeks, especially in the final days. At-the-money options have the largest theta in rupee terms because they carry the most time value. Deep in-the-money and far out-of-the-money options have smaller theta because they have less time value to lose.

Theta and gamma are two sides of the same trade-off. Buyers get positive gamma — the chance of profiting from sharp moves — and pay for it through negative theta. Sellers earn theta but take on negative gamma. Strategies such as covered calls and short strangles aim to collect theta, while long straddles pay theta in the hope of a big move.

A widespread misconception is that time decay happens only on trading days. Option pricing models treat time as continuous, so weekends and holidays also reduce time value, which markets typically price in before the break. Another is that selling options is 'free money' from theta; one large move can wipe out months of decay income.
items.example: A ₹1,000 strike at-the-money call with 30 days left, 20% volatility and 7% interest is worth about ₹25.79 by the Black-Scholes model. With 29 days left and nothing else changed, it is worth about ₹25.31 — a theta of roughly −₹0.48 per day. On a lot of 600, a buyer loses about ₹290 a day to time decay, and a seller gains the same, if the price stays put.
faqs: Which options lose value fastest due to time decay?

At-the-money options close to expiry lose time value the fastest in rupee terms, because their premium is entirely time value and the remaining time is short. Far out-of-the-money options lose a larger percentage of their small premium, often becoming nearly worthless in the last few days.
Is theta good for option sellers?

Theta works in favour of sellers because they gain as time value decays. But sellers take on negative gamma and face potentially large losses if the price moves sharply. Many experienced sellers use spreads or hedges to limit this risk rather than relying only on theta.

items.title: Option Vega Meaning: Volatility Sensitivity of Premiums
items.description: Vega explained with an example: how much an option's price changes when implied volatility moves by one percentage point, and why vega matters around events.
items.short: Vega measures how much an option's premium changes for a one percentage point change in the implied volatility of the underlying.
body: Higher volatility makes large price moves more likely, which raises the value of both calls and puts. Long options therefore have positive vega, and short options have negative vega. A vega of 1.13 means the premium rises by about ₹1.13 if implied volatility increases from, say, 20% to 21%, and falls by the same if volatility drops to 19%.

Vega is largest for at-the-money options and for options with more time to expiry. A three-month option is much more sensitive to volatility changes than a one-week option, because uncertainty compounds over time. This is why traders who want to bet on volatility often use longer-dated options.

Vega becomes critical around scheduled events — company results, RBI policy announcements, the Union Budget or elections. Implied volatility usually rises before the event and drops sharply afterwards. An option buyer who correctly predicts the direction can still lose if the drop in volatility reduces the premium more than the price move adds.

Vega is not a Greek letter at all; it was borrowed into options jargon. In exams, remember that vega is the same sign for calls and puts (positive for buyers) and that volatility is the only option pricing input that is not directly observable — it must be estimated or implied from market prices.
items.example: Using Black-Scholes, a 30-day ₹1,000 at-the-money call priced at 20% volatility is worth about ₹25.79. At 21% volatility it is worth about ₹26.92, so vega ≈ ₹1.13. Before a result announcement, IV rises from 20% to 28%: the call gains roughly 8 × ₹1.13 ≈ ₹9 even if the stock does not move. If IV falls back to 20% after results, that ₹9 disappears.
faqs: Do calls and puts have the same vega?

For European options with the same strike, expiry and underlying, call and put vegas are equal under the Black-Scholes model. Both gain when implied volatility rises and lose when it falls. This is why straddles, which combine a call and a put, have high vega.
Why do option prices fall after results even when the stock moves?

Implied volatility usually rises ahead of results because of uncertainty and then drops after the announcement. The drop reduces premiums through vega. If the stock's actual move is smaller than what the options had priced in, the loss from falling volatility can exceed the gain from the move.

items.title: Implied Volatility Meaning: IV, India VIX and Option Prices
items.description: What implied volatility is, how it is derived from option prices, how India VIX measures expected Nifty volatility and how to convert IV into expected moves.
items.short: Implied volatility is the market's expectation of future volatility of an underlying, backed out from current option prices using an option pricing model.
body: An option pricing model takes the spot price, strike, time, interest rate, dividends and volatility to produce a price. All inputs except volatility are known. If we take the actual market price of an option and solve for the volatility that produces it, we get implied volatility (IV). It is expressed as an annualised percentage.

Historical volatility looks backward, measuring how much prices actually moved. IV looks forward, reflecting what option buyers and sellers collectively expect, including fear and event risk. Different strikes often show different IVs — the 'volatility smile' or 'skew' — with out-of-the-money puts often carrying higher IV because of demand for downside protection.

India VIX, published by NSE, is a volatility index computed from Nifty option prices. It represents the expected annualised volatility of the Nifty over the next 30 days. A VIX of 15 suggests the market expects the Nifty to move within roughly ±15% over a year with about 68% probability, under normal-distribution assumptions. VIX tends to rise when markets fall sharply.

IV is not a forecast of direction; it only measures the expected size of moves. Another misunderstanding is treating IV as a fixed property of an option — it changes continuously with demand and supply. High IV makes options expensive for buyers and attractive for sellers, but it is high for a reason.
items.example: India VIX is at 15 and the Nifty is at 24,000. To estimate the one-month expected move, divide by √12: 15% ÷ 3.464 ≈ 4.33%. So one standard deviation over a month is about 24,000 × 4.33% ≈ 1,039 points — the market is pricing roughly a 68% chance that the Nifty stays between about 22,960 and 25,040, assuming a normal distribution.
faqs: Is India VIX the same as implied volatility?

India VIX is an index derived from the implied volatilities of near- and next-month Nifty option prices across several strikes. It summarises expected Nifty volatility for the next 30 days. Individual stock or strike IVs can be higher or lower than VIX.
Does high implied volatility mean the market will fall?

Not necessarily. High IV means a large move is expected but says nothing about direction. That said, IV and VIX often rise during market falls because demand for protective puts increases. A rising VIX is a sign of uncertainty, not a prediction of direction.

items.title: Put-Call Ratio (PCR) Meaning: Formula and Interpretation
items.description: Put-call ratio explained: calculating PCR from open interest or volume, what high and low PCR may indicate, and why it is often read as a contrarian sign.
items.short: The put-call ratio is the ratio of put options to call options traded or outstanding, used as an indicator of market sentiment.
body: PCR can be calculated in two ways. The open interest PCR divides total put open interest by total call open interest for an underlying, usually across all strikes of an expiry. The volume PCR divides the number of put contracts traded by the number of call contracts traded in a day. Both are widely published for the Nifty and Bank Nifty.

Interpretation depends on who is assumed to be active. If buyers dominate, a high PCR means many people are buying protection, suggesting bearish sentiment. But much of the open interest in Indian index options comes from sellers. Heavy put writing by sellers, who expect the market to stay above certain levels, also raises PCR — which is why some traders read a rising PCR as supportive.

Many traders use PCR as a contrarian indicator at extremes. A very high PCR may signal excessive pessimism and a possible rebound; a very low PCR may signal over-optimism. There is no universally correct threshold, and readings around 1 are often called neutral.

PCR should not be used in isolation. It does not distinguish hedgers from speculators, buyers from sellers, or near-the-money from far strikes. Combining it with price trend, open interest changes at specific strikes and implied volatility gives a more complete picture.
items.example: For the current weekly expiry, total put open interest is 1.2 crore contracts and total call open interest is 1.0 crore, so OI PCR = 1.2. Today's put volume is 45 lakh contracts and call volume 60 lakh, so volume PCR = 0.75. The two readings tell different stories: positions held overnight lean towards puts, while today's trading leaned towards calls.
faqs: What is a good put-call ratio?

There is no universally good value. Readings near 1 are often considered neutral. Some traders treat values well above 1 as signs of pessimism (and possible contrarian buying) and values well below 1 as signs of complacency. Thresholds vary by underlying and market conditions, so PCR is best compared with its own history.
Is PCR based on open interest more useful than volume PCR?

They answer different questions. Open interest PCR shows positions carried over, reflecting medium-term positioning. Volume PCR shows the day's activity, which can be noisy and include many intraday trades. Traders often track both and look for changes rather than absolute levels.

items.title: Black-Scholes Model: Option Pricing Inputs and Assumptions
items.description: Black-Scholes option pricing model explained simply: its inputs, the call and put formulas, key assumptions, limitations and a worked Indian stock example.
items.short: The Black-Scholes model is a mathematical formula that estimates the fair value of European options using the spot price, strike, time, interest rate and volatility.
body: Developed by Fischer Black and Myron Scholes in 1973, with contributions from Robert Merton, the model transformed option trading by providing a consistent way to price options. Scholes and Merton received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1997. Indian exchanges and brokers use Black-Scholes-based calculations to show theoretical prices, implied volatility and Greeks.

The call value is C = S × N(d1) − K × e^(−rT) × N(d2), and the put value is P = K × e^(−rT) × N(−d2) − S × N(−d1). Here S is the spot price, K the strike, r the risk-free rate, T the time to expiry in years, σ the volatility, and N() the cumulative normal distribution. d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r + σ²/2)T] ÷ (σ√T), and d2 = d1 − σ√T. N(d1) is the call's delta.

Its assumptions include: European exercise; no dividends (in the basic version); constant volatility and interest rate; continuous trading with no transaction costs; and log-normally distributed prices. Real markets violate several of these — volatility changes, prices sometimes jump, and costs exist — which is why market prices show a volatility smile.

In exams, focus on the inputs and direction of effects rather than computing by hand: a higher spot raises calls and lowers puts; higher volatility raises both; more time generally raises both; a higher interest rate raises calls and lowers puts. The model's practical use is less about the 'right' price and more about a common language for volatility and risk.
faqs: Can Black-Scholes be used for Indian stock options?

Yes. Indian equity options are European style, which suits the model. Practitioners adjust for expected dividends and use implied volatility from the market rather than a single historical figure. Exchange and broker option calculators commonly use Black-Scholes or close variants.
What is the biggest limitation of Black-Scholes?

The assumption of constant volatility. In reality, volatility changes over time and differs across strikes, creating the volatility smile or skew. Sudden jumps in prices, for example after unexpected news, are also not captured well. Traders deal with this by using different implied volatilities for different strikes.

items.title: Covered Call Strategy: Meaning, Payoff and Example
items.description: Covered call strategy explained: holding shares while selling call options for income, the payoff at different prices, maximum profit and the risks involved.
items.short: A covered call is an options strategy in which an investor holds the underlying shares and sells call options on them to earn premium income.
body: The strategy is called 'covered' because the shares owned cover the obligation if the call is exercised. The investor collects premium upfront. If the share price stays below the strike at expiry, the call expires worthless and the investor keeps both the shares and the premium. If the price rises above the strike, the shares are effectively sold at the strike price.

Maximum profit is capped at (strike − purchase price) + premium received. Downside is reduced only by the premium; if the share falls sharply, the investor still bears most of the loss. The breakeven at expiry is the purchase price minus the premium. The strategy suits a mildly bullish or neutral view.

Investors often sell out-of-the-money calls month after month to generate extra income from long-term holdings. Some mutual fund schemes in India are allowed to write covered calls on their equity holdings within SEBI's limits. Physical settlement of stock options means an in-the-money short call at expiry results in delivery of shares.

The main misconception is that covered calls are risk-free income. The real risks are giving up big upside rallies and still facing almost full downside in a crash. Taxes and transaction costs on frequent option writing also reduce net income.
items.example: Divya holds 500 shares bought at ₹1,200. She sells a one-month ₹1,260 call at ₹22, receiving ₹11,000. At expiry: at ₹1,230, the call expires worthless — share gain ₹15,000 plus ₹11,000 premium = ₹26,000. At ₹1,300, the call is exercised; her gain is capped at (₹60 × 500) + ₹11,000 = ₹41,000. At ₹1,150, the shares lose ₹25,000, partly offset by premium, so the net loss is ₹14,000.
faqs: When is a covered call a good strategy?

It suits investors with a neutral to mildly bullish view who are willing to sell their shares at the strike price. It works best when the stock moves sideways, letting the investor collect premium repeatedly. It is less suitable if a strong rally is expected, since gains above the strike are given up.
What is the maximum loss in a covered call?

The maximum loss occurs if the share price falls to zero: the loss on the shares minus the premium received. In formula terms, it is the purchase price minus the premium, multiplied by the quantity. The premium cushions only a small part of a big decline.

items.title: Protective Put Strategy: Meaning, Cost and Payoff
items.description: Protective put strategy explained: buying a put to insure shares you hold, how maximum loss is capped, the cost of protection and when investors use it.
items.short: A protective put is a strategy in which an investor who owns shares buys a put option on them to limit losses if the price falls.
body: The put works like an insurance policy. The premium is the insurance cost, the strike price is like the level of cover and expiry is the policy period. If the share falls below the strike, the put gains value and offsets the loss on the shares. If the share rises, the put expires worthless but the investor enjoys the full upside minus the premium.

The maximum loss is fixed: (purchase price − strike price + premium) × quantity. The breakeven at expiry is the purchase price plus the premium. Choosing the strike is a trade-off: a strike closer to the current price gives better protection but costs more; a lower strike is cheaper but leaves a bigger gap before protection starts.

Investors use protective puts before uncertain events, such as elections or major results, or when they want to keep a long-term holding but fear a short-term fall. Portfolio managers often buy index puts as a protective put on a diversified portfolio rather than buying puts on each stock.

The common mistake is buying protection continuously; repeated premium costs can significantly reduce long-term returns. Another is assuming the put protects beyond expiry — once it expires, the shares are unprotected. The payoff of a protective put resembles that of a long call, a relationship captured by put-call parity.
items.example: Vikram holds 400 shares bought at ₹2,500 (₹10,00,000). He buys a ₹2,400 put at ₹45 (₹18,000). If the share falls to ₹2,100, the shares lose ₹1,60,000, the put pays ₹1,20,000 and the net loss is ₹58,000 — his maximum, since (2,500 − 2,400 + 45) × 400 = ₹58,000. If the share rises to ₹2,800, he gains ₹1,20,000 less the ₹18,000 premium, i.e., ₹1,02,000.
faqs: Is a protective put the same as a stop-loss?

Both aim to limit losses, but they work differently. A stop-loss is free but may execute at a worse price in a gap-down and closes the position. A protective put costs premium but guarantees the right to sell at the strike until expiry, regardless of gaps, and lets you keep the shares if the price recovers.
How do I choose the strike for a protective put?

It depends on how much loss you can tolerate and how much premium you are willing to pay. An at-the-money put gives the most protection at the highest cost. An out-of-the-money put is cheaper but only protects after a larger fall. Compare the premium against the size of the protection gap.

items.title: Straddle vs Strangle Options Strategy: Meaning and Payoff
items.description: Long and short straddle and strangle strategies explained with Nifty-style examples: breakeven points, maximum loss, and when traders use each one.
items.short: A straddle combines a call and a put with the same strike and expiry; a strangle combines an out-of-the-money call and put with different strikes and the same expiry.
body: A long straddle means buying an at-the-money call and an at-the-money put. It profits from a large move in either direction and loses if the price stays near the strike. The maximum loss is the total premium paid, and there are two breakevens: strike plus total premium and strike minus total premium.

A long strangle uses an out-of-the-money call and an out-of-the-money put. It is cheaper than a straddle, but needs a larger move to become profitable, because the breakevens are further apart. Both are long-volatility strategies: they benefit if actual or implied volatility rises, and they suffer from time decay.

The reverse positions — short straddle and short strangle — involve selling the options. Sellers collect premium and profit if the price stays within the breakevens, but face large, theoretically unlimited losses on big moves. They are popular among option sellers in Indian index options, which is why SEBI's margin rules and expiry-day measures focus on short options.

Traders often buy straddles before events like results or the RBI policy, expecting a big move. The catch: option prices already include expected volatility, so implied volatility may fall after the event, and the move may not be large enough to cover the premium.
items.example: Index at 24,000. Long straddle: buy 24,000 call at 210 and 24,000 put at 190 — total 400 points, ₹30,000 for a lot of 75. Breakevens: 23,600 and 24,400. If the index expires at 24,900, the call is worth 900 and profit is 500 × 75 = ₹37,500. Long strangle: buy 24,300 call at 90 and 23,700 put at 80 — total 170 points (₹12,750) with breakevens at 24,470 and 23,530.
faqs: Which is better, a straddle or a strangle?

A straddle costs more but starts making money with a smaller move; a strangle is cheaper but needs a larger move. Choice depends on how big a move is expected and the price of options. For sellers, a short strangle gives a wider profit range but collects less premium than a short straddle.
What is the risk of a short straddle?

A short straddle profits only if the price stays within the two breakevens. A sharp move either way can cause large losses, theoretically unlimited on the upside. It also has high negative gamma, especially near expiry, so losses can grow quickly. Sellers often use stop-losses or buy far options to cap risk.

items.title: Currency Futures Meaning: USD-INR Futures in India
items.description: How currency futures work on Indian exchanges: USD-INR and other pairs, contract size, cash settlement at the RBI reference rate and hedging by importers.
items.short: Currency futures are exchange-traded contracts to buy or sell a fixed amount of foreign currency at a set exchange rate on a future date, settled in rupees.
body: Exchange-traded currency futures started in India in 2008 with USD-INR contracts on NSE, followed by BSE and MSE. Contracts are available on USD-INR, EUR-INR, GBP-INR and JPY-INR, and cross-currency pairs such as EUR-USD, GBP-USD and USD-JPY. The market is jointly regulated: the RBI sets the policy framework for currency derivatives, while SEBI regulates exchanges and brokers.

A standard USD-INR futures contract is for USD 1,000, quoted in rupees per dollar up to four decimal places. Contracts are cash settled in rupees — no dollars change hands. Final settlement uses the RBI reference rate on the last trading day, which is typically two working days before the last business day of the month. Daily mark-to-market applies like other futures.

Importers buy USD-INR futures to protect against a rising dollar; exporters sell them to protect against a falling dollar. Exchange-traded contracts are transparent and accessible to smaller businesses that may not get good forward rates from banks. RBI rules on who can take positions and whether an underlying exposure must be shown have changed over time, so check the current RBI directions on exchange-traded currency derivatives.

A confusion to avoid: a rise in the USD-INR rate means the rupee has weakened (more rupees per dollar). Another is assuming currency futures let you hold foreign currency; they are cash-settled contracts used for price risk, not a way to move money abroad.
items.example: An importer must pay USD 50,000 in two months. USD-INR futures for that month trade at 84.20. She buys 50 contracts (50 × USD 1,000). At expiry, the RBI reference rate is 85.10. Her futures gain (85.10 − 84.20) × 50,000 = ₹45,000, offsetting the higher cost of buying dollars in the spot market. Her effective rate stays close to 84.20, apart from basis and costs.
faqs: Are currency futures settled in dollars?

No. Currency futures on Indian exchanges are cash settled in Indian rupees. Only the difference between the contract rate and the final settlement rate is paid or received. To actually buy dollars, a business must still go through its bank, but the futures gain or loss offsets the rate change.
What is the RBI reference rate?

It is the official rupee exchange rate published by the RBI (through FBIL, the benchmark administrator) each business day for major currencies. Exchanges use it to settle currency futures and options at expiry, ensuring an independent and transparent final settlement price.

items.title: Interest Rate Futures Meaning: Bond Futures in India
items.description: What interest rate futures are, how 10-year government bond futures work in India, why prices fall when yields rise, and how banks use IRFs to hedge.
items.short: Interest rate futures are exchange-traded contracts whose value depends on the price of an interest-bearing instrument, such as a government bond or treasury bill.
body: In India, interest rate futures (IRFs) trade on NSE and BSE on underlyings such as 10-year Government of India bonds and 91-day treasury bills, with other tenors introduced from time to time. They are regulated by SEBI for exchange trading, within the framework set by the RBI. Bond futures are typically cash settled based on the weighted average price of the underlying bond.

The key relationship is inverse: when interest rates (yields) rise, bond prices fall, and so do bond futures. A bank holding government bonds can sell IRFs to protect against rising yields. A fund expecting to receive money and invest in bonds later can buy IRFs to lock in today's yields.

How much a bond price moves for a given change in yield is measured by modified duration. A bond with modified duration 7 falls about 7% if yields rise by 1 percentage point. Hedgers use duration to work out how many IRF contracts they need: hedge ratio = (portfolio value × portfolio duration) ÷ (futures value × futures duration).

The market is mostly used by banks, primary dealers, insurers and mutual funds. Liquidity in Indian IRFs has been uneven, which limits retail use. Students often get the direction wrong — remember: expectation of rising rates means sell bond futures; expectation of falling rates means buy them.
items.example: A 10-year bond future trades at ₹100.00 per ₹100 face value, and the contract size is ₹2 lakh face value. A trader expecting yields to rise sells 10 contracts (₹20 lakh face value). Yields rise by 0.25 percentage point; with a modified duration of 7, the price falls about 1.75% to ₹98.25. Profit ≈ ₹20,00,000 × 1.75% = ₹35,000, before costs.
faqs: Why do bond futures fall when interest rates rise?

Existing bonds pay fixed coupons. When new bonds offer higher yields, older bonds become less attractive, so their prices drop until their yield matches the market. Bond futures track these prices, so they fall too. The opposite happens when interest rates fall.
Who uses interest rate futures in India?

Banks, primary dealers, insurance companies, mutual funds and some corporates use them to hedge interest rate risk on bond portfolios or future borrowings. Traders and arbitrageurs also participate. Retail participation has been limited because of the specialised nature of the product and uneven liquidity.

items.title: Commodity Futures Meaning: MCX and NCDEX Contracts Explained
items.description: How commodity futures work in India on MCX and NCDEX: gold, crude oil and agri contracts, delivery and cash settlement, and how farmers and jewellers hedge.
items.short: Commodity futures are exchange-traded contracts to buy or sell a standard quantity and quality of a commodity at a fixed price on a future date.
body: India's main commodity derivatives exchanges are MCX, which leads in bullion, energy and base metals, and NCDEX, which focuses on agricultural commodities. Since the Forward Markets Commission merged with SEBI in September 2015, commodity derivatives have been regulated by SEBI under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act.

Each contract specifies the commodity, quantity, quality grade, delivery centre and settlement method. For example, a gold contract may cover 1 kg, while smaller 'mini' and 'petal' variants exist for smaller traders. Many agricultural contracts are compulsory delivery, settled through exchange-accredited warehouses, while energy contracts such as crude oil are generally cash settled against international benchmark prices.

Hedgers include farmers and farmer producer organisations who sell futures before harvest, processors and millers who buy futures to lock in raw material costs, and jewellers who hedge gold inventory. Options on commodity futures and options on goods have also been introduced, giving hedgers insurance-like tools.

Commodity prices are influenced by global factors — weather, OPEC decisions, the rupee-dollar rate and international prices. Traders sometimes forget that domestic gold and crude futures embed both international prices and the exchange rate. Also, commodity contracts have their own daily price limits and margins, separate from equity rules.
items.example: A cotton ginner expects to buy 100 bales in three months and fears a price rise. Cotton futures trade at ₹57,000 per bale (illustrative). She buys futures for 100 bales. At expiry, cotton is ₹60,500. She pays ₹3,500 more per bale in the physical market (₹3,50,000 extra) but gains about ₹3,50,000 on futures, keeping her effective cost near ₹57,000 per bale, apart from basis differences between her local market and the exchange delivery centre.
faqs: Who regulates commodity derivatives in India?

SEBI, since the Forward Markets Commission was merged into it in September 2015. Commodity exchanges such as MCX and NCDEX and their clearing corporations are recognised under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act. Physical warehouse standards are also overseen as part of the exchange and clearing corporation framework.
Do I have to take delivery in commodity futures?

It depends on the contract. Many agricultural contracts are compulsory delivery, so open positions at expiry lead to delivery through accredited warehouses. Others are cash settled. Some contracts give options to deliver. Always read the contract specifications before trading close to expiry.

items.term: SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India)
items.title: What is SEBI? Role, Powers and Functions Explained
items.description: SEBI meaning and role: how the Securities and Exchange Board of India regulates markets, its three types of powers, and appeals to SAT.
items.short: SEBI is India's statutory regulator for the securities market, set up to protect investors' interests and to develop and regulate the market.
body: SEBI was formed in 1988 as a non-statutory body and received statutory powers through the SEBI Act, 1992. Its headquarters is in Mumbai. The board has a chairperson, two members from the Union Finance Ministry, one from the RBI and five other members, of whom at least three are whole-time members. Before SEBI, capital issues were controlled by the Controller of Capital Issues.

The SEBI Act's preamble sums up its three aims: protecting the interests of investors, promoting the development of the securities market, and regulating it. SEBI registers and supervises intermediaries — stock brokers, depositories, DPs, mutual funds, portfolio managers, investment advisers, research analysts, merchant bankers, RTAs and others — and regulates listed companies' disclosures, takeovers and insider trading.

SEBI has three types of powers. Quasi-legislative: it frames regulations. Executive: it inspects, investigates and enforces rules. Quasi-judicial: it passes orders, imposes penalties and can bar entities from the market. Appeals against SEBI orders go to the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT), and then to the Supreme Court.

SEBI does not guarantee investment returns or approve the merit of any security. It also does not regulate everything financial: banks fall under the RBI, insurance under IRDAI, pensions under PFRDA. Since 2015, commodity derivatives have also been under SEBI.
items.example: A listed company fails to disclose a material default to the exchanges on time. SEBI examines the case, issues a show-cause notice and, after a hearing, an adjudicating officer imposes a penalty on the company and its compliance officer. The company appeals to SAT, which may uphold, modify or set aside the order; a further appeal can go to the Supreme Court. This flow shows SEBI's executive and quasi-judicial roles in action.
faqs: When was SEBI established?

SEBI was established on 12 April 1988 as a non-statutory body through a government resolution. It became a statutory body with the SEBI Act, 1992, which gave it legal powers to regulate the securities market. This distinction between formation and statutory status is a common exam question.
Where can I appeal against a SEBI order?

Appeals against SEBI orders lie with the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT), generally within 45 days of receiving the order, subject to condonation for delay. Orders of SAT can be appealed before the Supreme Court on questions of law. SAT also hears appeals against orders of IRDAI and PFRDA.

items.title: KYC Meaning in Securities Market: Process and KRA
items.description: What KYC means for investors in India, documents needed, in-person and video verification, KYC registration agencies and why a KYC can be on hold.
items.short: KYC is the process by which a regulated entity verifies the identity, address and other basic details of a customer before opening an account or providing services.
body: KYC is required under the Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002 and its rules, and by SEBI's master circulars for intermediaries. Its purpose is to make sure that financial services are not misused by people hiding their identity, and that intermediaries understand their clients well enough to monitor suspicious activity.

For securities markets, the investor provides PAN (compulsory), proof of identity and address — for example Aadhaar, passport or voter ID — a photograph and contact details. Verification is done in person, by video-based in-person verification or through Aadhaar-based e-KYC. Brokers also collect income range, occupation and, for derivatives trading, proof of financial capacity.

SEBI created KYC Registration Agencies (KRAs) so investors need to complete KYC only once across intermediaries. After one intermediary uploads the KYC, the KRA validates key attributes such as PAN, name, address, mobile number, email and income range. Others can then fetch the record. A KYC can show statuses like 'registered', 'validated' or 'on hold', and an on-hold KYC blocks new investments until fixed.

KYC is not a one-time event. Intermediaries must periodically update KYC, more often for high-risk clients, and update records when details change. A common misconception is that a bank KYC automatically covers the securities market — it usually needs to be validated with a KRA or CKYC, even if details match.
items.example: Sana opens a trading account with a broker using Aadhaar e-KYC and PAN. The broker uploads her KYC to a KRA, which validates her PAN with the income tax database and her email and mobile through OTPs, marking the KYC 'validated'. A year later, she invests through a mutual fund platform; it fetches her KRA record and lets her invest without repeating the full process.
faqs: What is a KRA?

A KYC Registration Agency is a SEBI-registered entity that stores and validates KYC records of investors in the securities market, so they don't have to repeat KYC with each intermediary. CVL (CDSL Ventures), NDML (NSDL), CAMS, KFintech and NSE's KRA are examples. Intermediaries upload and fetch records from KRAs.
Why is my KYC on hold?

Common reasons are mismatch between PAN and Aadhaar details, unverified email or mobile number, PAN not linked with Aadhaar, or incomplete documents. You can check status on any KRA website using PAN and correct the issue through your broker, DP or mutual fund platform.

items.title: CKYC Meaning: Central KYC Number (KIN) and How It Works
items.description: What CKYC is, how the CERSAI-run Central KYC Records Registry works across banks, insurers and brokers, the 14-digit KIN and how it differs from KRA KYC.
items.short: CKYC is a central repository of customer KYC records, run by CERSAI, that lets customers complete KYC once and use it across banks, insurers, securities intermediaries and pension funds.
body: The Central KYC Records Registry was set up under the Prevention of Money-laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, and the government authorised the Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest of India (CERSAI) to operate it. Entities regulated by the RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA must upload KYC records of new customers to the CKYC registry.

Each customer gets a 14-digit KYC Identification Number (KIN), also called the CKYC number. When the customer approaches another regulated entity, that entity can download the record using the KIN or other identifiers instead of collecting all documents again, though it may still verify details and collect additional information required for its own risk assessment.

CKYC and KRA KYC co-exist in the securities market. KRAs handle KYC specific to SEBI intermediaries, while CKYC spans the entire financial sector. SEBI has required intermediaries to upload records to CKYC as well, and has worked on interoperability between the two systems.

People sometimes think CKYC replaces all verification. It reduces paperwork but does not stop an institution from carrying out enhanced due diligence for higher-risk customers. Another misconception is that the KIN is secret like a password; it is an identifier, though it should still be shared only with genuine financial institutions.
items.example: Farhan opened a savings account in 2022, and the bank uploaded his KYC to CKYC, generating a 14-digit KIN. In 2026 he buys a term insurance policy online. The insurer searches CKYC using his PAN, downloads his record and only asks him to confirm his current address and upload a selfie. He completes the purchase without resubmitting identity documents.
faqs: How can I find my CKYC number?

Your CKYC number (KIN) may be mentioned in an SMS or email from CERSAI or from the institution that uploaded your KYC. Banks and some financial platforms can also look it up using your PAN. Some third-party sites offer searches, but use only trusted official or institutional channels.
Is CKYC the same as KRA KYC?

No. KRA KYC is specific to SEBI-regulated intermediaries in the securities market, managed by KYC registration agencies. CKYC is a central registry across banking, insurance, securities and pensions, run by CERSAI. Many investors have both, and regulators are working on making them interoperable.

items.title: PMLA Meaning: Money Laundering Rules for Intermediaries
items.description: Prevention of Money-laundering Act explained for securities market intermediaries: stages of laundering, reporting to FIU-IND, CTRs, STRs and record-keeping.
items.short: The Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002 is India's main law to prevent money laundering and to confiscate property derived from crime.
body: PMLA came into force on 1 July 2005. It applies to banks, financial institutions and intermediaries such as stock brokers, depositories, DPs, mutual funds, portfolio managers and RTAs, which are called 'reporting entities'. They must verify client identity, maintain records of transactions, and report certain transactions to the Financial Intelligence Unit–India (FIU-IND).

Money laundering is usually described in three stages: placement (introducing illegal cash into the financial system), layering (moving it through many transactions to hide the source), and integration (bringing it back as apparently legitimate wealth). Securities markets are vulnerable mainly at the layering and integration stages, for example through rapid trades, off-market transfers or using third-party accounts.

Key obligations include client due diligence, identifying beneficial owners, risk categorisation of clients, ongoing monitoring, filing cash transaction reports (CTRs) and suspicious transaction reports (STRs), and maintaining records for at least five years after the business relationship ends. Each entity must appoint a Principal Officer for reporting and a Designated Director responsible for compliance.

A frequent misconception is that PMLA only concerns cash. Most securities market transactions are cashless, yet the law still applies, and suspicious patterns such as unusual third-party payments, sudden large trades inconsistent with income, or links to sanctioned persons must be reported.
items.example: A broker's monitoring system flags a new client who declared annual income of ₹4 lakh but deposits ₹65 lakh from three different bank accounts over two weeks, buys a thinly traded stock and requests withdrawal to a fourth account. The Principal Officer reviews the alerts, finds no satisfactory explanation, and files an STR with FIU-IND, without informing the client — tipping off is prohibited.
faqs: What is FIU-IND?

The Financial Intelligence Unit–India is the central national agency that receives, analyses and disseminates information on suspicious financial transactions. It works under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance. Reporting entities file CTRs and STRs with FIU-IND through its online system.
How long must records be kept under PMLA?

Reporting entities must keep records of transactions and of client identity for at least five years — transaction records from the date of the transaction and identity records from the end of the business relationship. SEBI's guidelines may require longer retention in some cases, so check the current master circular.

items.title: Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) Meaning and Timeline
items.description: What a suspicious transaction report is, red flags in securities trading, the timeline for filing with FIU-IND, and why tipping off the client is prohibited.
items.short: A suspicious transaction report is a report filed by a regulated entity with FIU-IND about a transaction or attempted transaction that appears linked to money laundering or terrorist financing.
body: Under PMLA rules, a transaction is suspicious if, to a person acting in good faith, it gives reasonable grounds to suspect proceeds of crime, appears unusually complex, has no apparent economic rationale, or may involve terrorist financing. There is no minimum amount — even a small transaction can be suspicious, and attempted transactions that were not completed must also be reported.

The Principal Officer of the intermediary must file the STR with FIU-IND within seven working days of being satisfied that the transaction is suspicious. The clock starts from the date of that conclusion, not from the date of the trade, so alerts must be reviewed promptly. Reasons for the conclusion should be documented.

Typical red flags in securities markets include clients whose trading volumes are far beyond declared income, frequent payments from unrelated third parties, trades in illiquid stocks at prices far from the market, sudden activation of dormant accounts, off-market transfers without clear reasons, and clients reluctant to provide KYC information.

Two rules are critical. The intermediary must not tip off the client that an STR has been filed, and it should continue the relationship normally unless there are other reasons to stop. Filing an STR is not an accusation — it is information for FIU-IND to analyse along with other data.
items.example: On 3 June, a DP's surveillance system flags a client who received shares worth ₹48 lakh by off-market transfer from five unrelated accounts and sold them within two days. The compliance team investigates and, on 10 June, concludes the pattern is suspicious. The Principal Officer must file the STR within seven working days of 10 June — the date of that conclusion, not the 3 June alert or the original transfers.
faqs: Is there a minimum amount for filing an STR?

No. Unlike cash transaction reports, which have thresholds, an STR has no minimum value. Any transaction, of any size, that gives reasonable grounds for suspicion must be reported, including attempted transactions that were abandoned or rejected by the intermediary.
Can the client be told that an STR was filed?

No. Disclosing that an STR has been or will be filed is called tipping off and is prohibited. Staff must keep the information confidential. The intermediary may continue dealing with the client normally while FIU-IND and other agencies examine the report.

items.title: Beneficial Owner Meaning: UBO Thresholds Under PMLA
items.description: Who is a beneficial owner or ultimate beneficial owner under PMLA rules, ownership thresholds for companies and trusts, and how intermediaries identify UBOs.
items.short: A beneficial owner is the natural person who ultimately owns or controls a client account, or on whose behalf a transaction is conducted, even if the account is in another entity's name.
body: When a client is a company, partnership, trust or other entity, intermediaries cannot stop at the entity's name. Under PMLA rules and SEBI circulars they must identify the individuals behind it — the ultimate beneficial owners (UBOs). This prevents criminals from hiding behind layers of shell companies.

For a company, a beneficial owner is a natural person who, alone or together with others, owns more than a specified percentage of shares or capital, or exercises control through other means such as voting agreements or the right to appoint directors. The thresholds were tightened in 2023 to more than 10% for companies and partnership firms (as of 2026 — check the current PML Rules and SEBI circulars). For trusts, the settlor, trustees, protector, beneficiaries with a defined stake and anyone with ultimate control are identified.

If no individual crosses the threshold and no one exercises control by other means, the senior managing official is treated as the beneficial owner. Intermediaries must verify the identity of UBOs, keep records and update them when ownership changes.

In depository terms, 'beneficial owner' also has a different, narrower meaning: the person whose name appears in the demat account as entitled to the securities, as opposed to the depository, which is the registered owner. Exam questions can test either meaning, so read the context carefully.
items.example: A private company opens a trading account. Its shareholding: Holding Co. A (60%), Mr. Rao directly (8%), others (32%). Holding Co. A is owned 50% by Ms. Mehta and 50% by Mr. Rao. Indirect stakes: Ms. Mehta 30% and Mr. Rao 30% + 8% = 38%. Both exceed 10%, so both are beneficial owners whose KYC the broker must collect and verify.
faqs: Why do intermediaries need to identify beneficial owners?

Without identifying the real individuals behind an entity, it would be easy to use shell companies or trusts to hide illegal money or evade sanctions. Identifying UBOs lets intermediaries assess risk properly, screen against sanctions lists and report suspicious activity linked to the true controllers.
Is the beneficial owner the same as the account holder?

Not always. For an individual, the account holder is usually the beneficial owner. For a company or trust, the account is in the entity's name, but the beneficial owners are the natural persons who ultimately own or control it. In depository law, the demat account holder is called the beneficial owner.

items.title: Politically Exposed Person (PEP) Meaning and Due Diligence
items.description: Who counts as a politically exposed person, why PEPs are treated as high-risk clients, enhanced due diligence steps and senior management approval in India.
items.short: A politically exposed person is an individual who holds or has held a prominent public function, such as a senior politician, judge or military official, and who therefore needs enhanced due diligence.
body: Under SEBI's anti-money laundering guidelines and PMLA rules, PEPs are individuals entrusted with prominent public functions by a foreign country or within India — for example heads of state or government, senior politicians, senior government or judicial or military officers, senior executives of state-owned corporations and important political party officials. The definition is broad, and intermediaries also apply similar care to family members and close associates.

PEPs are not presumed to be criminals. They are treated as higher risk because their position could be misused for bribery or corruption, and because laundering proceeds of corruption often involves such individuals. International standards set by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) require extra checks on them.

Enhanced due diligence includes approval from senior management before opening the account (or continuing it if an existing client becomes a PEP), taking reasonable steps to establish the source of wealth and funds, and conducting closer ongoing monitoring of transactions. The client must be categorised as high risk.

A common mistake is thinking that PEP status ends the moment a person leaves office. Risk-based approaches often keep former PEPs under enhanced monitoring for a period, and status of relatives and close associates also needs attention.
items.example: A retired senior civil servant opens a demat and trading account and wants to transfer ₹2 crore of shares from another DP. The broker's screening flags him as a PEP. The compliance team obtains senior management approval, asks for documents on the source of the shares and wealth (inheritance records and past salary statements), categorises him as high risk and sets tighter alert thresholds on his transactions.
faqs: Can an intermediary refuse to open an account for a PEP?

PEP status alone is not a reason to refuse. Intermediaries must apply enhanced due diligence and take a risk-based decision. If they cannot satisfactorily establish the source of funds or the client refuses to cooperate, they may decline the relationship and, where appropriate, consider filing a suspicious transaction report.
Do family members of PEPs also need enhanced checks?

Yes. Regulators and FATF guidance expect intermediaries to apply similar enhanced due diligence to family members and close associates of PEPs, because they may be used to hold or move funds on the PEP's behalf. The extent of checks follows the intermediary's risk assessment.

items.title: Insider Trading Meaning: SEBI PIT Rules and Penalties
items.description: What insider trading is under SEBI's Prohibition of Insider Trading Regulations, who is an insider, prohibited acts, disclosures, contra trades and penalties.
items.short: Insider trading is dealing in a company's securities while in possession of unpublished price sensitive information (UPSI), or communicating such information without a legitimate purpose.
body: Insider trading in India is governed by the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, often called the PIT Regulations. An 'insider' is any connected person — directors, employees, auditors, advisers and others with access to the company — or anyone in possession of or with access to UPSI. A person does not need to be an employee to be an insider; a friend who receives a tip can be one.

The regulations prohibit two things: trading when in possession of UPSI, and communicating or procuring UPSI except for legitimate purposes, performance of duties or legal obligations. Companies must maintain a structured digital database of people with whom UPSI is shared and a code of conduct for designated persons.

Designated persons face additional rules. They cannot trade when the trading window is closed, need pre-clearance for trades above a threshold, must disclose trades above a value threshold within a short time, and cannot do a contra trade (opposite trade) within six months of a previous trade. Trading plans approved in advance provide a defence for insiders who need to trade regularly.

Penalties are severe: under Section 15G of the SEBI Act, the penalty can be up to ₹25 crore or three times the profit made, whichever is higher, besides disgorgement of gains, market bans and possible criminal prosecution. A misconception is that trading through a relative's account avoids detection; SEBI routinely analyses trading patterns, call records and relationships.
items.example: A finance manager learns on 5 April that the quarterly profit will be 40% below estimates, to be announced on 20 April. On 8 April, his brother-in-law sells 10,000 shares at ₹620. After results, the share falls to ₹520. The loss avoided is ₹10 lakh. If SEBI establishes that UPSI was shared, both can be penalised — up to ₹25 crore or three times the ₹10 lakh gain, whichever is higher — and the gain disgorged.
faqs: Is it illegal to trade on a tip from a friend who works at a company?

Yes, if the tip contains unpublished price sensitive information. Under SEBI's PIT Regulations, anyone in possession of UPSI is treated as an insider, whether or not they work for the company. Trading on such information, or passing it on, can attract penalties for both the tipper and the person who trades.
What is a contra trade under insider trading rules?

A contra trade is a trade in the opposite direction — for example, selling shares within six months of buying them. Designated persons are prohibited from contra trading within six months. If they do, any profit must be disgorged and transferred to SEBI's Investor Protection and Education Fund, unless relaxation is granted.

items.title: UPSI Meaning: Unpublished Price Sensitive Information
items.description: What counts as unpublished price sensitive information under SEBI rules, examples like results and mergers, and when information becomes public.
items.short: UPSI is information about a company or its securities that is not generally available and that, if made public, is likely to materially affect the share price.
body: The SEBI PIT Regulations give an illustrative list of UPSI: financial results, dividends, changes in capital structure, mergers, demergers, acquisitions, delistings, disposals and expansion of business, and changes in key managerial personnel. Later amendments added items such as fraud or defaults by the company, resolution plans and significant orders. Companies also judge other information on its likely price impact.

Information becomes 'generally available' when it is published in a way that gives investors non-discriminatory access — typically through disclosure to the stock exchanges. Media speculation does not make information public; a leak in a news report is still UPSI until the company formally discloses it.

Companies must control the flow of UPSI. They share it only on a 'need-to-know' basis, maintain a structured digital database recording who received UPSI and when, and use non-disclosure agreements with advisers. Chinese walls separate teams that handle UPSI from teams that trade or advise clients, especially in financial firms.

A common confusion is to treat all non-public information as UPSI. Routine operational details are not price sensitive. The test is whether the information would be likely to materially affect the price. Another misconception is that analysts' estimates are UPSI; analyses built from public information are not, but selective disclosure of non-public data to analysts can be.
items.example: A listed cement company's board is negotiating to acquire a competitor for ₹4,500 crore. The deal team, legal advisers and two bankers know about it; each is entered in the structured digital database. A news portal reports rumours of 'a large acquisition'. Until the company informs the exchanges after board approval, details of the deal remain UPSI, and anyone in the database is barred from trading the shares.
faqs: When does UPSI stop being unpublished?

When it becomes generally available, which usually means the company has disclosed it to the stock exchanges or through another method that gives the public equal access. Insiders should wait until the market has had a reasonable opportunity to absorb the information before trading, consistent with the company's code of conduct.
Can UPSI be shared with lenders or investors during a deal?

Yes, for legitimate purposes, such as due diligence for a transaction, provided confidentiality agreements are signed and the recipients are recorded in the structured digital database. Recipients then become insiders and cannot trade in the company's securities until the information becomes public.

items.title: Trading Window Closure Meaning for Designated Persons
items.description: What the trading window is under SEBI insider trading rules, when it closes around quarterly results, who it applies to and what designated persons cannot do.
items.short: The trading window is the period during which a company's designated persons and their relatives are permitted to trade in its securities; it is closed when they may have access to UPSI.
body: Under the SEBI PIT Regulations, every listed company's compliance officer manages the trading window. For financial results, the window closes from the end of every quarter until 48 hours after the results are declared. The company can also close the window at other times when designated persons are expected to have UPSI, such as during a major acquisition.

The rule applies to designated persons — directors, key managerial personnel, employees in finance, legal and other sensitive functions identified by the board — and to their immediate relatives. While the window is closed, they cannot trade in the company's securities, even if they personally have no UPSI.

When the window is open, designated persons still need pre-clearance from the compliance officer for trades above the threshold in the company's code, must complete pre-cleared trades within a set number of trading days, and must avoid contra trades within six months. Trades under an approved trading plan can be carried out despite window closure, subject to conditions.

Many employees think that only those who actually know the results are barred. The window closure is a blanket rule meant to remove any doubt. Another misconception is that buying ESOP shares through exercise is always restricted; exercising options is generally allowed during closure, but selling the shares is not.
items.example: A company's quarter ends on 30 June and its board declares results on 8 August at 5 p.m. The trading window for designated persons is closed from 1 July until 48 hours after the announcement, i.e., until 10 August at 5 p.m., so trades can resume from the next trading session after that. A finance manager who buys 500 shares on 15 July violates the code, even if he did not see the numbers.
faqs: Who has to follow trading window restrictions?

Designated persons identified by the company's board — such as directors, key managerial personnel and employees with access to sensitive information — and their immediate relatives. The company's code of conduct lists the categories. Others who come to possess UPSI are still covered by the general prohibition on insider trading.
Can a designated person trade during closure under a trading plan?

Yes. SEBI's regulations allow trades under a trading plan that was approved and publicly disclosed in advance, because the trades were decided before the insider had the UPSI. Trading plans have conditions about cool-off periods and duration, so they must be set up carefully.

items.title: Front Running Meaning in Stock Market: Rules and Examples
items.description: What front running is, how dealers or brokers trade ahead of large client or fund orders, why SEBI treats it as fraud, and examples of how it is detected.
items.short: Front running is trading in a security ahead of a known large pending order from a client or fund, to profit from the price movement that order is likely to cause.
body: Large orders move prices. A dealer who knows that a mutual fund will buy 20 lakh shares of a stock in the afternoon can buy the same stock earlier — in their own name or through a relative — and sell it to the fund or in the market after the price rises. The profit comes directly at the cost of the client, who pays a higher price.

SEBI treats front running as a fraudulent and unfair trade practice under the PFUTP Regulations. It applies to anyone who has access to non-public information about large orders, including employees of brokers, fund houses, insurance companies and custodians, and anyone they share the information with. Intermediaries must have policies to prevent it, such as restricting personal trading and recording dealer calls.

Detection relies on trade surveillance. Regulators look for accounts that repeatedly buy just before a large order and sell during or just after it, often in matching quantities, and link them through phone records, IP addresses and family relationships. Several SEBI orders in recent years have involved dealers of fund houses and their relatives.
