Front running is different from insider trading, though both misuse confidential information. Insider trading concerns company-specific UPSI, while front running concerns knowledge of pending orders. It also differs from legitimate trading on public news, which anyone may do.
items.example: A fund house dealer receives an order to buy 10 lakh shares of a mid-cap at around ₹300. Before placing it, he tips a friend, who buys 50,000 shares at ₹300. The fund's large order pushes the price to ₹309, and the friend sells at an average ₹308. Profit: ₹8 × 50,000 = ₹4 lakh, which effectively came out of the fund investors' pockets through the higher purchase price.
faqs: Is front running the same as insider trading?

No, though both are prohibited. Insider trading uses unpublished price sensitive information about a company. Front running uses knowledge of an upcoming large order. Both are forms of misuse of confidential information, but they are covered by different regulations: PIT Regulations and PFUTP Regulations respectively.
How do intermediaries prevent front running?

They restrict and monitor personal trading by employees, require pre-approval of personal trades, record dealer phone lines, use surveillance to flag trades ahead of client orders and separate dealing teams from others. SEBI also requires fund houses to have an institutional mechanism to deter and detect such misconduct.

items.title: Market Manipulation Meaning: SEBI PFUTP Rules Explained
items.description: What market manipulation means under SEBI's PFUTP Regulations: circular trading, pump and dump, spoofing, misleading tips and the red flags to watch.
items.short: Market manipulation is any deliberate act that distorts the price or volume of a security to mislead other investors, prohibited under SEBI's PFUTP Regulations.
body: The SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices relating to Securities Market) Regulations, 2003 — usually called PFUTP — prohibit any manipulative, fraudulent or deceptive device in connection with dealing in securities. The rules list examples but are deliberately broad so that new schemes can be caught.

Common forms include circular trading, where a group trades among itself to create artificial volume; synthetic or reversal trades with no change in beneficial ownership; pump and dump schemes, where operators buy a cheap stock, spread rumours or 'tips' through social media or messaging apps, and sell at inflated prices; spoofing, where large orders are placed with no intention to execute; and marking the close to influence closing prices.

SEBI uses exchange surveillance, data analytics and social media monitoring to detect manipulation, and can impose penalties, disgorgement, trading bans and refer cases for prosecution. SEBI has also restricted associations between regulated entities and unregistered 'finfluencers' who give stock recommendations, as these have been used in pump and dump schemes.

Investors often think a sharp rise in volume and price signals good news. In small and illiquid stocks, such moves — especially with aggressive promotions on messaging groups — can be manipulation. Exchange surveillance measures such as ASM/GSM lists and tighter price bands are useful warning signs.
items.example: Operators accumulate 20 lakh shares of a small company at around ₹12. They then trade among their own accounts, pushing volume from 50,000 shares a day to 15 lakh, while promoting the stock on messaging channels with claims of a 'big order win'. The price rises to ₹38. They sell 18 lakh shares to new investors at an average ₹35 — a gain of about ₹4.1 crore — before the price collapses back towards ₹14.
faqs: What is circular trading?

Circular trading is when a group of connected people repeatedly buy and sell a security among themselves to create an impression of active trading and price movement, without any real change in ownership. It misleads other investors about liquidity and demand. SEBI treats it as a manipulative practice under the PFUTP Regulations.
How can I protect myself from pump and dump schemes?

Be wary of unsolicited stock tips on social media or messaging groups, especially for small, illiquid companies. Check company disclosures on exchange websites, look at surveillance lists, and avoid buying because of sudden volume spikes alone. Remember that SEBI-registered advisers and analysts must disclose their registration numbers.

items.title: SEBI SCORES Meaning: How to File an Investor Complaint
items.description: What SEBI SCORES is, how to lodge a complaint against a listed company or intermediary, SCORES 2.0 timelines, review levels and what it cannot handle.
items.short: SCORES is SEBI's online complaints redress system where investors lodge and track complaints against listed companies and SEBI-registered intermediaries.
body: SEBI launched SCORES in 2011 to bring complaints online and make their handling transparent. An upgraded version, SCORES 2.0, was introduced in 2024 with auto-routing of complaints, shorter timelines and two levels of review. Investors can file complaints through the website or mobile app after registering with their PAN and contact details.

Under the framework, the entity concerned must resolve the complaint within 21 calendar days of receipt (as of 2026 — check the current SEBI circular). If the investor is not satisfied, a first-level review is done by a designated body, such as the relevant stock exchange or depository. If still unresolved, the investor can request a second review by SEBI.

Typical complaints include non-receipt of dividend or shares, problems with transfer or transmission, unauthorised trades by a broker, delays in refund or allotment, and service deficiencies by mutual funds or DPs. SCORES does not handle complaints that are sub-judice, already under arbitration, or that concern entities not regulated by SEBI, such as unregistered tipsters or chit funds.

A misconception is that SEBI will award compensation through SCORES. SCORES pushes the entity to resolve the grievance; it is not a court. If a dispute is not resolved, the investor may move to online dispute resolution (ODR), which can result in a binding arbitral award.
items.example: Neha's dividend of ₹3,600 from a listed company was not credited because of an old bank account. She first writes to the RTA; after 10 days with no reply, she files on SCORES. The company must respond within 21 days; it updates her bank details and pays the dividend on day 14. Had the response been unsatisfactory, she could seek a first review by the exchange and then a SEBI review.
faqs: Do I have to contact the company before filing on SCORES?

Investors are expected to first approach the listed company or intermediary directly. If the grievance is not resolved or there is no response, they can file on SCORES. Complaints should generally be filed within the time limit SEBI specifies from the date of the cause of action.
Can SCORES award me compensation?

No. SCORES is a complaint tracking and escalation system. It ensures the entity responds and resolves the complaint, and lets SEBI monitor and act against non-compliance. For a binding monetary decision on a dispute, investors can use the online dispute resolution mechanism or approach courts.

items.title: SEBI ODR Portal Meaning: Online Dispute Resolution Process
items.description: How SEBI's online dispute resolution works: the Smart ODR portal, conciliation and online arbitration, who can use it, timelines and fees for investors.
items.short: Online dispute resolution is SEBI's mechanism for resolving disputes between investors and listed companies or market intermediaries through online conciliation and arbitration.
body: SEBI introduced a common ODR framework in 2023, creating the Smart ODR portal linked to SCORES. It covers disputes with stock brokers, depository participants, mutual funds, investment advisers, research analysts, listed companies and many other regulated entities. An investor can initiate ODR after first approaching the entity, if the grievance is not resolved satisfactorily — with or without having gone through SCORES.

The process has two stages. First, an independent conciliator appointed by an empanelled ODR institution tries to help the parties reach a settlement through online meetings. If conciliation fails, the investor can move to online arbitration, where an arbitrator hears both sides and passes a binding award under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

SEBI prescribes timelines: conciliation is to be completed within about 21 days (extendable on request) and arbitration within about 30 days of appointment, as of 2026 — check current circulars. Fees for investors are kept low and depend on the claim size, while the intermediary bears a share of costs. Intermediaries must also be able to initiate ODR against clients.

ODR does not apply to disputes already in court or claims time-barred under law, and it is not available against unregistered entities. Investors sometimes confuse ODR with SCORES; SCORES is complaint handling, ODR is formal dispute resolution leading to a binding outcome.
items.example: Rohit claims his broker squared off his positions without a margin call, causing a ₹1.8 lakh loss. The broker rejects his complaint. Rohit files on the Smart ODR portal. In conciliation, the broker offers ₹60,000, which he declines. He opts for arbitration; after reviewing the margin records and call logs, the arbitrator awards him ₹1.2 lakh, which the broker must pay within the timeline set by the award.
faqs: Is the ODR outcome binding?

A settlement reached in conciliation is binding once both parties sign it. An arbitral award passed by the arbitrator is binding and enforceable like a court decree under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, though it can be challenged on limited grounds before a court.
Can I use ODR without going through SCORES?

Yes. The investor should first take up the grievance directly with the entity. If unresolved, the investor may go to SCORES or directly to the ODR portal. Using SCORES is not mandatory before ODR, though many investors try it first because it is free.

items.title: Investor Protection Fund (IPF) Meaning and Broker Defaults
items.description: What a stock exchange's investor protection fund is, when investors can claim compensation after a broker default, claim limits, timelines and what it covers.
items.short: An investor protection fund is a fund maintained by each stock exchange and depository to compensate investors for eligible claims when a member defaults.
body: Stock exchanges are required by SEBI to set up an investor protection fund (IPF), usually managed through a trust. Its main purpose is to pay valid claims of investors against a trading member who is declared a defaulter or expelled. Depositories maintain a similar fund for claims arising from DP defaults. The funds are financed by contributions from exchanges, fees and penalties.

When a broker is declared a defaulter, the exchange publishes notices inviting claims within a specified period. A committee examines each claim to verify that it relates to genuine trades on the exchange, settled or unsettled obligations, or securities and money held with the broker in the normal course of business. Approved claims are paid up to a per-investor limit set by the exchange in line with SEBI guidelines; the limit is revised from time to time, so check the exchange website.

The IPF does not cover losses from market movements, from trading on bad advice, or from transactions that were not on the exchange, such as private deals, assured return schemes or loans to the broker. Claims also need documentary support such as contract notes, ledger statements and bank records.

Students often confuse the IPF with the settlement guarantee fund. The Core SGF guarantees settlement between clearing members, protecting the system. The IPF compensates individual investors for losses caused by their broker's default. SEBI also maintains its own Investor Protection and Education Fund, which supports investor education and can be used for refunds in certain cases.
items.example: A broker is declared a defaulter. Meera had a credit balance of ₹3.4 lakh in her ledger and 200 unpaid-for shares worth ₹1.1 lakh that the broker had not delivered after she paid. She files a claim with contract notes and bank statements within the claim period. The committee verifies both items, and since the ₹4.5 lakh total is within the exchange's per-investor limit, she is paid in full from the IPF.
faqs: Does the investor protection fund cover trading losses?

No. The IPF covers genuine claims arising from a member's default, such as money or securities the broker owed the investor. It does not compensate for losses due to price movements, poor investment decisions, or dealings outside the exchange system such as assured-return schemes.
How long do I have to file a claim after a broker default?

Exchanges publish a notice inviting claims and specify a period for filing. SEBI's guidelines allow claims to be filed within a prescribed period from the date of the notice, with some flexibility for delayed claims in genuine cases. Check the exchange's defaulter notice for the exact deadline.

items.title: Takeover Code and Open Offer: SEBI SAST 25% Trigger
items.description: How SEBI's takeover code works: the 25% open offer trigger, creeping acquisition, minimum 26% offer size, offer price rules and disclosure thresholds.
items.short: The takeover code, SEBI's Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers (SAST) Regulations, 2011, requires an acquirer crossing set thresholds to make an open offer to public shareholders.
body: The idea is fairness: when control of a listed company changes or someone builds a large stake, public shareholders should get a chance to exit at a fair price. An acquirer who, alone or with persons acting in concert, acquires 25% or more of voting rights must make an open offer. Acquiring control, even without crossing 25%, also triggers an offer.

Holders already between 25% and the maximum permissible non-public shareholding (75%) can acquire up to 5% more voting rights in a financial year without an open offer — the creeping acquisition limit. Beyond that, an open offer is required. The open offer must be for at least 26% of the total shares of the company.

The offer price must be at least the highest of several benchmarks, including the negotiated price under the agreement that triggered the offer, the volume-weighted average price paid by the acquirer in the preceding 52 weeks, the highest price paid in the preceding 26 weeks, and the 60-trading-day volume-weighted average market price for frequently traded shares. A merchant banker manages the offer and an escrow account secures payment.

The code also requires disclosures: anyone crossing 5% must disclose, and further changes of 2% or more must be disclosed. Promoters must disclose their holdings and encumbrances. A misconception is that an open offer means the acquirer must buy all public shares — the minimum is 26%, and acceptance can be proportionate if more is tendered.
items.example: Company X has 10 crore shares. An acquirer buys 26% (2.6 crore shares) from the promoter at ₹180 per share, crossing 25%. It must make an open offer for at least another 26% — 2.6 crore shares — at no less than the highest benchmark price, say ₹192 (the 60-day VWAP). If public shareholders tender 4 crore shares, acceptance is proportionate at 65%; if all goes through, the acquirer ends at 52%.
faqs: What is creeping acquisition?

Creeping acquisition lets a shareholder who already holds 25% or more, but less than the maximum permissible non-public shareholding, acquire up to 5% additional voting rights in a financial year without making an open offer. It allows gradual consolidation while still requiring an open offer for faster or larger acquisitions.
Do I have to tender my shares in an open offer?

No, participation is voluntary. Shareholders can tender all, some or none of their shares. If more shares are tendered than the offer size, the acquirer accepts them proportionately. Shareholders who do not tender continue to hold their shares in a company with a new or stronger controlling shareholder.
